payload.close_reason: fixed: per-path regenerate commands plus a conflict-marker guard, so a partly generated file is declarable (cb715ff)
payload.description:
## Context

The merge queue already has the right mechanism for a generated artifact
(`basicly-lyro`): a path in `[worktree] generated_paths` is not merged, both sides are
discarded and `regenerate_command` rebuilds it from the tree the rebase produced. Measured
2026-08-08, it covers exactly one file:

```text
generated_paths    = [".basicly/generated-manifest.json"]
regenerate_command = ["basicly", "build"]
```

`docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` carries a second generated artifact - a
`<!-- docs-claims:begin plan-current-state -->` block written by `.scripts/docs_claims.py`
holding the module count, the test-file count and the verify-check counts. Every lane that
adds a module or a test file changes it, and it conflicted on the 2026-08-08 pass.

## Two reasons the one-line fix is wrong

1. **The file is only partly generated.** The rest is hand-authored ladder prose. The
   mechanism discards *both sides*, so declaring the whole path would destroy
   hand-written changes on any lane that also edited the prose.
2. **`basicly build` cannot rebuild it.** `.scripts/docs_claims.py` is referenced from
   `basicly.toml` as a `[[verify.checks]]` entry with a `fix_command`, and from **nowhere
   in `src/basicly/`** - so the declared `regenerate_command` is a no-op for this block.

So the block must move to its own included file (or the regeneration must become
block-scoped), **and** `docs_claims.py --fix` must be reachable from the regenerate path,
before the path is declared.

## Steps to Reproduce

```text
$ grep -n 'generated_paths' basicly.toml
103:generated_paths = [".basicly/generated-manifest.json"]

$ grep -rn 'docs_claims' src/basicly/
(no output - the declared regenerate_command cannot rebuild the block)
```

Observed on pass `basicly-u2hl:bc7cc925`, 2026-08-08: two lanes each added a source
module, the second rebased, `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` conflicted on the
docs-claims counts, and the lane bounced back for a re-dispatch.

Expected: the block is a function of the tree, so the rebase should discard both sides and
rebuild it, as it already does for `.basicly/generated-manifest.json`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given two lanes that each add a source module, when the second rebases onto the first,
  then the docs-claims block is rebuilt from the merged tree rather than bouncing the lane
  - check: a merge-queue test lands two branches that each add a module and asserts zero
  rework recorded and a block whose counts match the merged tree.
- Given a lane that edits hand-authored prose in the same file, when it lands, then that
  prose survives - check: a test asserts an edited prose line is present after the
  regeneration path runs.

## Demonstration

`uv run python .scripts/docs_claims.py --check` passes on the merged tree after a
two-lane landing that would previously have bounced.

## Scope

- `basicly.toml`
- `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md`
- `.scripts/docs_claims.py`
- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`
- `tests/test_docs_claims.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `80000`
- depends on: none
payload.title: Rebuild the generated docs claims block at landing instead of bouncing the lane

payload.text:
[harness-info] paid again, and by hand, 2026-08-14

The lane landing basicly-5p49 hit a rebase conflict on exactly the block this bead names. Two lanes forked from the same base, both regenerated the generated block in `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md`, and neither value was correct after the merge:

```text
feje  87 modules, 157 test files, 24 checks
5p49  86 modules, 158 test files, 25 checks
truth 87 modules, 159 test files, 25 checks
```

I resolved it by deleting both sides and running `docs_claims.py --fix`, which is what `[worktree] generated_paths` would have done automatically for any path listed there. That list holds one entry, `.basicly/generated-manifest.json`, with `regenerate_command`.

So the bead is now witnessed rather than predicted. The remedy is one line: add the plan to `generated_paths` and give it `docs_claims.py --fix` as its regenerate command. Note the two paths need different commands, so the config has to carry a command per path or the plan needs its own entry.

The cost of not having it, measured here: one aborted merge, one hand-resolved rebase, and a regenerated block that neither lane could have produced alone.

Every concept in §3, §4, §5 and §12 holds; the five dispositions P1–P5 in §11.3 do not move. Ten citations in `docs/research/2026-08-17-deepseek-harness.md` are wrong at the pin they name:

- line 484-485: `run-gates.ts` "909 lines … topologically sorts them (`visit` at `:694`)" — `visit` is the DFS inside `findDependencyCycle` (:744/:750), a cycle detector; ordering is the scheduler loop at :813; 968 lines.

- line 649: "14 CI workflows" — 18 (§13.4 already says so); line 978 "exactly two tags" — 4 (§13 already corrects it).

The `docs-citations` gate reports 29 of 41 citations unverifiable; a citation into an external repository is one of them, so this class recurs on every pin move with nothing to catch it. - WHEN §7's durable-state or cost row is read, IT SHALL mention the PR #2730 state/view split in one sentence with its Agent Note path, and §11.3 SHALL record that P3's basis is unchanged by it.
- WHEN `uv run basicly verify --mode fast` runs, `docs-citations` SHALL be green and its unverifiable count SHALL not rise.
- Demonstrated by: `uv run python .scripts/docs_citations.py` (or the check's own command from `basicly.toml`) on the edited document.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a declared verify check that the engine has run and passed when the exercised-or-unproven gate evaluates a release then that check counts as exercised and does not block the tag and given a declared check that nothing has ever run then the gate still refuses and names it and a test fails if a wrapper executable rather than the check itself is accepted as the witness
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

Measured 2026-08-05 on `main` @ `d31f6bd`, a clean tree, immediately after
`uv run basicly verify --mode full` reported **PASS, 16 checks — `vulture: PASS`**:

```
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from basicly import release
print(release.unexercised_capabilities(Path('.')))"
```

Observed — one refusal, for a check that had just run and passed in the same session:

```
unexercised capability: verify check 'vulture' - the usage ledger records no
execution of 'vulture'; exercise it or drop the claim before tagging
```

The per-capability read, over 17 declared checks against a ledger holding 544 keys:

| witness | count | capability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vulture` | **0** | verify check `vulture` |
| `uv` | 6091 | verify check `wired-or-deleted`, `docs-claims` |
| `ruff` | 711 | verify check `ruff`, `ruff-format` |
| `pytest` | 785 | verify check `pytest` |
| `basicly` | 2963 | the five `projection-*` checks |

Expected — a declared check that the engine ran, and that passed, counts as exercised.

## Consequence: v0.7.0 cannot be tagged

`release.blocking_reasons` extends with `unexercised_capabilities` (`release.py:382`),
and by that function's own docstring the reasons are checked **before anything is
written**. So `basicly release` refuses the cut, and no amount of re-running `verify`
changes the answer. This is a release blocker for `basicly-yc0x`, not a cleanup item.

## Cause: the witness is a typed shell command, not an execution

`shipped_capabilities` derives each witness as the check's own `command[0]`
(`release.py:252`). `recorded_executions` (`release.py:257`) reads two ledgers, and
neither one can see a check the engine ran:

- `usage.load_usage` reads `.basicly/usage/tool-usage.json`, written by the
  `tool-usage` hook (`.basicly/core/hooks/hooks.yaml:80`), which counts **pipeline
  heads of Bash commands an agent executed**. `vulture` is never typed at a shell —
  it exists only as a `[[verify.checks]]` entry — so its counter is never created.
- `tracker_usage.surface_executions` is the committed half and carries tracker
  surfaces, not verify checks.

`src/basicly/verify.py` records nothing: it has no reference to `usage` at all. So the
one component that actually executes a declared check is the one component that never
witnesses it. Every other check passes only because a human or an agent happened to
type its executable for unrelated reasons.

## The same defect makes the gate vacuous in the other direction

`wired-or-deleted` is declared as `uv run python .scripts/...`, so its witness is `uv`
with 6091 executions — a count that would stay healthy if the check were deleted
outright. `shipped_capabilities`' docstring already names this ("witnessed by the
*wrapper*, which is weaker evidence") and defers the fix to the declaration. It is not
a declaration problem: both facets are one cause, a witness that measures who typed a
word rather than whether the capability ran. A gate that is simultaneously
unsatisfiable for one check and unfalsifiable for another is measuring the wrong event.

## Fix shape

- **`verify` records an execution for each check it runs**, and `recorded_executions`
  reads that as a third ledger half. The engine running the check is the strongest
  available evidence that the capability works — it is the only evidence that the
  check *passed* rather than merely being invoked — and it makes the witness the
  check's `name`, which is unique per declaration, instead of `command[0]`, which is
  shared and wrapper-prone.
- **Do not satisfy this by typing `vulture` once at a shell.** That mints a false
  witness for a capability the gate cannot otherwise see, and leaves the next
  engine-only check blocked in exactly the same way. **Do not drop the claim either** —
  `vulture` is a live gate that `basicly-uexy` shipped deliberately.
- Keep the fail-closed stance on a missing ledger: that half is correct and
  `unexercised_capabilities`' docstring gives the reason.
- Regression test proven red first (`basicly-kjc5.49`): a declared check the engine has
  run is exercised; a declared check nothing has ever run still refuses the tag.

## Context

`basicly-uexy` (which declared `vulture`) and `basicly-irrm` (which built this gate)
shipped in the **same four-lane pass** on 2026-08-04. Neither lane could see that one
was declaring a capability the other's witness model cannot record. This is Phase S's
own shape one turn later — an instrument built and connected to the wrong signal — and
it is the fourth instance of the rule that a closed bead proves code exists, not that a
gate binds. Here the gate does bind; it binds on the wrong event, and it binds against
us.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/release.py`
- `src/basicly/verify.py`
- `src/basicly/usage.py`
- `tests/test_release.py`
- `tests/test_verify.py`

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given recorded pipeline heads containing heredoc delimiters and language keywords when usage report runs then the tool table lists only resolvable command names and unparsed heads are counted to a named bucket and the counter file is not reset
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
uv run basicly usage report | head -40
```

Observed 2026-08-04 - the terminal-tools table counts things that are not tools. Among the top
entries: `t` (123), `-` (121), `-d` (120), `def` (90), `assert` (83), `create` (70), `run` (65),
`from` (51), `p` (43), `PYEOF` (33), `return` (31), `EOF` (28). These are heredoc delimiters, Python
keywords and flag fragments picked up as pipeline heads. Expected - the table lists commands.

## Context

`usage report` exists to support a decision: the `session-finish` skill reads its **never-used**
list as the culling candidates for catalog skills. Pollution on the tools half undermines that in
both directions - it invents tools that were never run, and a real command parsed as a fragment is
undercounted or missed entirely, so a genuinely-unused tool can look used.

The skills half of the report is clean and its finding is sound and worth keeping: **8 skills used
ever, 27 never used**, including every `tool-*` skill. That is the same shape as
`basicly-irrm`'s inventory result (221 dispatch records hold only `claude` and `manual` while the
README advertises three agents), and it is real evidence for the culling `basicly-a3ab.1` and
`basicly-tcmy.21` carry.

This is the defect class `basicly-never-used-can-be-fabricated` names: in a usage audit the
never-used side is the only one a measurement bug can invent. So the *tools* half of this report may
not be cited as evidence until the parser is fixed; the *skills* half may.

## Fix shape

- Extract pipeline heads by parsing the command, not by splitting on whitespace: skip heredoc bodies
  and their delimiters, and skip anything that is not a resolvable command name.
- A recorded head that matches no known executable and no catalog entry is a parser miss - count it
  to a bucket the report names, rather than into the tool table as if it were real.
- Do **not** reset the counter file to clear the noise; it accumulates across sessions by design and
  the historical rows are the fixture for the fix.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/hooks/`
- `src/basicly/usage.py`
- `tests/test_usage.py`
payload.title: Usage report counts heredoc and keyword fragments as terminal tools

payload.description:
## Context

Four unattended-run attempts on 2026-08-05/06 failed, and three of them on the same
shape: two lanes editing one anchor in a shared prose file.

| Attempt | Blocked on |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | `CHANGELOG.md` — three lanes at the same `### Fixed` anchor |
| 3 | `.basicly/generated-manifest.json` — fixed by `basicly-lyro` |
| 4 | `docs/design/tier-injection-kit.md` §7 Open — two lanes each removing their own entry |

`basicly-o8p0` and `basicly-lyro` each fixed one instance by declaring the path. That
approach cannot finish: nobody predicted a design document's Open list, and detection
will always trail the next unenumerated file.

## The fix

**One file per lane, assembled at release.** A lane writes `changelog.d/<bead-id>.md`
instead of editing `CHANGELOG.md`. The filename carries the bead id, so it is unique by
construction and two lanes cannot touch the same file — collision becomes impossible
rather than detected. `basicly release` assembles the fragments into the dated section
in a deterministic order and deletes them.

This is the established news-fragment pattern; the point here is not novelty but that it
removes the cause instead of reporting it.

## What it composes with, and what it costs

`basicly release` already promotes the `[Unreleased]` body into the dated section, so
assembly replaces that read rather than adding a step. The costs are real and accepted:
the landing convention changes for every lane, the release runbook changes, and
`[worktree] append_only_paths` loses its only entry — which is the point, not a
regression.

Keep `[Unreleased]` working for hand-written entries during the transition: a release
assembles fragments **and** any curated body, so an operator editing the changelog
directly is never broken.

## Acceptance evidence to produce

A supervised pass of three lanes that each add a changelog entry must land all three
with no rebase conflict on any changelog path — the direct inverse of attempt 1.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/release.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `basicly.toml`
- `tests/test_release.py`
- `.basicly/core/skills/harness-loop/skill.yaml`
- `.basicly/core/skills/release-process/skill.yaml`
payload.title: Give every lane its own changelog fragment so two lanes can never collide on one anchor

system *is*, and `basicly-pip9` and `basicly-miqr` cover the plan and both requirements
documents. **Nothing covered `architecture.md` itself.** A start-of-session read on 2026-08-14
found eight claims false against the tree, and four capabilities the document never carried.

## What was false

1. §14.3 "The judgment layer — designed, unbuilt." Refuted: `roles.resolve_role` reaches an argv
   from three call sites (`loop.py:818`, `loop.py:1062`, `supervise.py:2749`) and six of the seven
   loop roles are reachable.
2. §0 pillar 3 and §12.2 omit VALIDATE from the loop and name the retro as a rung.
   `config.LOOP_PHASES` carries `validate`; the retro is not in `loop._HANDLERS` by decision.
3. §12.3 "**scheduling** … basicly reimplements none of these." Ranking is owned
   (`kit/tracker/scheduler.py` behind `br.read_ranking`, `basicly.scheduler.v1`) and harness
   markers are native.
4. §14.2 points at `factory-design.md` §9 as the authoritative reconciliation. That file is
   deleted and lost tiebreaker authority under D24.
5. §7 detail 1 says three scoped fragments; §14.4 says two. There are **four**.
6. §7 detail 1 argues the codex cap as an allowance. `codex.yaml:9` moved it 12000 to 16000
   after the `basicly-a3ab.1` audit found the overrun is structural to the scoped tier.

   dispatch` as `building`; both ship.

map; the handoff artifact schemas; RETROSPECTIVE on a computed special cause; the improvement
controller. All six are running code.

## The finding, which outlives the fix

A `[[verify.checks]]` entry gates the two generated blocks in this document and **nothing checks
its prose against the tree**. `basicly-pip9` and `basicly-miqr` are the same defect in three
other files, so this is the fourth instance of one class rather than a one-off — which is what

payload.text:
Doc check 2026-07-16 (VS Code 1.129, code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/agent-skills):
- Workspace roots scanned: .github/skills, .claude/skills, .agents/skills (user-level: ~/.copilot, ~/.claude, ~/.agents). Still NO documented dedup/precedence across roots. One secondary source claims .github/skills wins over .claude/skills on duplicates - unverified, and irrelevant here since we retired .github/skills; the pair that matters is .claude vs .agents.
- chat.agentSkillsLocations only ADDS locations; no documented setting to exclude a built-in root, so the copilot-side root-restriction option may not exist.
- 1.129 surfaces skills as slash commands and in a Configure Skills menu (/skills), plus the Agent Customizations editor (Chat: Open Customizations) - duplicates are now user-visible in three places.
- 1.129 also starts migrating prompt files (*.prompt.md) to skills (chat.customizations.promptMigration.enabled) with deprecation direction: validates the skills-first catalog design; basicly projects no prompt files, nothing to migrate.

Updated test procedure (basicly repo open in VS Code >= 1.129):
1. Copilot Chat: type / and look for conventional-commits - listed once or twice?
2. Run /skills (Configure Skills menu) - count entries per skill and note the source path shown for each.
3. Chat: Open Customizations - check the skills section the same way.
4. Context-level check: invoke one skill, expand the Used n references dropdown - did one or both SKILL.md paths load?
Record the VS Code + Copilot Chat versions with the result.

RESOLVED empirically 2026-07-16 by the user (VS Code 1.128.1, current Copilot Chat, WSL remote): Agent Customizations shows 27 of our skills - exactly 26 catalog skills (present byte-identically in BOTH .claude/skills and .agents/skills, 52 SKILL.md files on disk) plus the claude-only release-process skill. No duplicates listed, so VS Code dedups (or merges) same-named skills across roots. Keeping both roots stands: Claude Code reads only .claude/skills, Codex only .agents/skills, and Copilot presents one entry. No basicly-side change needed.

Bonus finding: the VS Code agent harness also consumes .claude/settings.json - our protect-generated PreToolUse hook and the user-level settings both appear under Hooks in Agent Customizations, so the 84v.3 tool-time guard gates Copilot's agent too, not just Claude Code.

payload.description:
## Context

Surfaced by `basicly-svct4w` the moment its fix let the provenance fold read engine written edges at all.

`provenance.py` expects the key to carry `EXTRACTED`, `INFERRED` or `AMBIGUOUS`. The engine writes
`engine` (`owned_write.OWNED_PROVENANCE`) and `dual-write` (`mirror.MIRROR_PROVENANCE`). One key, two
vocabularies that were never reconciled.

Measured consequence: **142 assertions carry a label the fold does not know** and are disposed as decide
rather than gating, which is why `gating_edges` reads 932 of 1065 rather than all of them. It is fail
closed, so nothing is wrongly gated today - but a third of the population is unusable and the reason is
a name collision rather than a missing fact.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Fold the committed ledger's edge events through `provenance.fold_edges`.
2. Count the assertions disposed as decide rather than gating.
3. Observe 142 of them, and observe each carries `engine` or `dual-write` in the provenance key.
4. Read `provenance.py`'s expected vocabulary and observe neither value is in it.
5. Observe `gating_edges` returns 932 of 1065, the difference being exactly the undecidable set.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an edge whose provenance key carries an engine written value when the fold reads it then the value is understood or the key is split so the two vocabularies do not share one name - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_kit_tracker_provenance.py -k vocabulary -q`
- Given the reconciliation then gating edges accounts for every folded edge or names why one is withheld

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/provenance.py`
- `tests/test_kit_tracker_provenance.py`

## Working Set

- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/provenance.py`
- `tests/test_kit_tracker_provenance.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest -q`
payload.title: the provenance payload key carries two unrelated vocabularies so a hundred and forty two assertions are undecidable

payload.text:
Closed by the commit above. Full verify PASS, 31 checks, 4488 tests.

gating_edges reads 1065 of 1065, up from 932. Disposed decide: 0. unknown_labels: empty. The 142 events are now counted in a new EdgeFold.writer_labels as engine 70 and dual-write 72.

CORRECTION - this record's 142 was right and I was wrong to doubt it. I measured 133 and reported the record as wrong. 142 counts EVENTS in unknown_labels; 133 counts distinct edges after last-statement-wins folding. The record says 142 assertions, and an assertion is an event. I read the narrower population and called the record's number a defect.

The two writer values gate because of what they mean: an event the engine's own seam appended is one a command asked for, which is EXTRACTED's claim. Two EXACT strings, not a prefix and not a fallback - a near miss still routes a decision, asserted, because a prefix match here would be a fail-open on the one gate deciding whether an edge may hold up a landing. Blast radius measured before the change: gating_edges has no production consumer, only one test in test_policy.py, so resolving the 133 could not start gating anything today.

The kit cannot import basicly, so the agreements it must hold are pinned from the test side: WRITER_LABELS == {owned_write.OWNED_PROVENANCE, mirror.MIRROR_PROVENANCE} and KEY_LABEL == migrate.PROVENANCE_KEY. A later split of the key fails there first.

The split this needed: provenance.py 7890 -> 6686 with labels.py at 2979. A real gain beyond the size - provenance and differential now read ONE DIALECT_KEYS table instead of two copies, which is basicly-oii83r's root cause removed rather than patched on both sides.

Two standalone-kit fixtures refused the new module until it was named, on the one constraint the kit cannot check from inside. Both now derive the file list from the directory by glob instead of enumerating it: a hand list was a second place the kit's shape was written down, and those two fixtures were the only thing that noticed labels.py was missing.

Not done: the key is still shared. This makes the second vocabulary legible; it does not split the key. Splitting it is a wire-format change to what the engine stamps on every event, and 142 committed events already carry the old spelling.

Pre-release sweep 2026-09-12, while checking whether other scanners shared the pyright blind spot.

The bandit check scanned `.scripts`, `.basicly/core/hooks` and `.basicly/core/kit`. `test_bandit_scans_every_harness_python_directory` derives its population from `_HARNESS_PYTHON_ROOTS`, which listed `.scripts` and `.basicly/core`. The coverage claim was bounded by the list it iterates, which is the rule the quality-gate fragment already states.

Nothing today: bandit was clean on `packages` when the directory was added. It buys the next edit.

## Verified
A deliberately unsafe module under `packages` now fails the scan with B602 and the tree is green once it is removed.

## Scope
- `basicly.toml`
- `tests/test_verify.py`

## Trigger
Pre-release audit 2026-09-12. `basicly-yhhmoqq` added a projected catalog content type with a schema, a builder, a checker, a verify gate and an install step, and `docs/architecture/architecture.md` had zero mentions of it.

## Why it matters
That file is named in the always-on instructions as the authoritative architecture reference. Every other content type has a section: 13 fragments, 14 skills, 15 subagents, 16 hooks, 17 model tiers, 18 permissions. A reader looking for how output styles project would find nothing and reasonably conclude the catalog does not own them.

Two how-to guides were also stale: the drift sequence in `upgrade-and-check-drift.md` listed five checks and not `styles-check`, and the rebuild/check table in `customize-the-catalog.md` listed five outputs and not the output-styles root.

## Root cause
The change added a verify gate and a CLI verb, and `wired-or-deleted` plus `docs-claims` both passed, because the CLI reference table was updated. No gate binds a new content type to a section in the architecture document, so the omission was invisible.

## Fix
Section 14A documents the root, the source shape, the schema, why `keep_coding_instructions` defaults to true, why the generated marker sits in the frontmatter rather than the body, the commands, and what stays hand-edited. Both how-to guides updated.

## Worth considering separately
A gate that refuses a new projected output path that no architecture section names. Not filed as work; recorded so the question is not lost.

## Scope
- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`
- `docs/how-to/upgrade-and-check-drift.md`
- `docs/how-to/customize-the-catalog.md`

## Context

Found by the lane-B survey 2026-08-14.

The exempted cycle at `.importlinter:58` has three deferred imports in `loop.py`, not one.

```text
loop.py:699    from . import supervise    reaches supervise.meter_context_ceiling   LIVE
loop.py:753    from . import supervise    reaches admit_working_set                 DEAD SPELLING
loop.py:2297   from . import supervise    reaches escalate_working_set              DEAD SPELLING
```

Both admission functions already moved to `working_set.py` and survive in `supervise` only as re-exports at `supervise.py:93-98`. `working_set` sits three tiers below `loop`, so a top-level import is legal today. `cli.py` also reaches four calls through the re-export, at `cli.py:2722`, `:2746`, `:2753` and `:2968`.

## Why this is first

`basicly-tcmy.13` carries an acceptance criterion that `loop` does not import `supervise` at any point. Today that criterion reads as move two functions and a meter. After this, it reads as move the meter. The bead shrinks by two thirds and the remaining work becomes nameable.

The `ignore_imports` entry stays until the meter moves. Its alerting mode is error, so it forces its own removal at that point. Leave it.

## Acceptance

- When the import graph is computed, then `loop` contains exactly one deferred `supervise` import, at the meter call.
- When the layering contract runs, then it passes unchanged.
- When `supervise.admit_working_set` and `supervise.escalate_working_set` are searched under `src/`, then nothing is returned.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`

## Warning

Declare a working-set subset. The three files read whole breach the band ceiling.

## Demonstration

`rg -c "from . import supervise" src/basicly/loop.py` prints 1, and `uv run pytest tests/test_supervise.py -q` passes.

payload.description:
## Context

`basicly usage report` names never-used catalog skills as culling candidates. The counter behind
it is the `tool-usage` PostToolUse hook, which counts **`Skill` tool invocations**.

`basicly-ey58` (shipped 2026-08-13) made a role's declared `skills:` reach its dispatch as
injected prompt content. An injected skill is never invoked through the Skill tool, so it never
increments the counter.

Measured on 2026-08-13, immediately after ey58 landed: the never-used list names
`validate-as-consumer`, `repair-in-place`, `decompose-plan` and `root-cause` - and all four are
declared by a loop role and delivered on every matching dispatch. The report recommends culling
skills that are actively used.

payload.description:
## Context

The loop names a persona per state and a skill per phase. **Neither exists in code.**
Measured 2026-08-08:

```text
rg -n -w -i 'dana|kai|vera|remo|juno|lumi|tala' src/basicly/   ->  0 hits
```

Seven personas designed (`agent-roster-design.md:225-303`), zero implemented — one default
runner serves every phase (`factory-loop-requirements.md:249`, `loop.py:678`). Of the five
skills in `flr` section 7, only `python-guidelines` exists; `decompose-plan`,
`validate-as-consumer`, `repair-in-place` and `root-cause` are each marked
**"nothing (gap)"** in the design and absent from `.basicly/core/skills/`.

And the three agents we *do* vendor are inert: `.claude/agents/` holds `code-reviewer`,
`security-auditor` and `test-runner`, written by `agents.sync()`, and **no dispatch code
reads that directory** — its only other consumer is `cli.py:1261`, which globs it to delete
files.

## The ordering decision this reverses, and why

`implementation-plan.md:469` records personas as *"deliberately **not** filed yet: D5's
rule admits a persona only when it differs in tier, tools or artifact, and **the artifacts
do not exist**"*. That gate has now partly opened: `basicly-u2hl.18` shipped
`implementation-plan` and `change-summary` as typed artifacts, and `u2hl.20` added the
demonstration field. So Dana (produces `implementation-plan`) and Kai (produces
`change-summary`) now differ by **artifact** and satisfy D5's own admission test.

Vera, Remo, Lumi and Tala still do not — their artifacts (`validation-transcript`,
`release-record`) are unbuilt. **This bead admits only the personas that pass the test**,
and records the others as blocked on their artifact rather than filing them speculatively.
Admitting all seven would be the accretion R3 exists to prevent.

## Constraints that must hold

- **Catalog sources, never hand-written `.md`.** Author under `.basicly/core/agents/<name>/
  agent.yaml` against `schemas/agent.schema.json`, reusing `agents/blocks/*.block.yaml`;
  `basicly catalog lint` enforces it and `.claude/agents/` is projected output.
- **Vendored to consumers.** These must reach a consumer through `basicly install`, not
  exist only here. If agents are not currently vendored by install, that gap is part of
  this bead and must be stated rather than assumed.
- **Agent-agnostic.** `agent-roster-design.md:210` forbids role prompts being Claude
  subagent files. Whether that survives is `basicly-xjd2`'s question; until it is answered
  this bead authors catalog sources that project to every root, which is compatible with
  both outcomes.
- **Each judged role carries an explicit adversarial stance** and a role-specific list of
  how *that* role goes soft. The roster requires these be **derived from recorded verdict,
  rework and adjudication history**, not invented — a generic "be rigorous" instruction is
  a no-op that costs tokens. Where history is too thin, say the list is asserted.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the projected catalog, when the agent roots are built, then each admitted persona
  is present in every root - check: `uv run basicly agents-build && uv run basicly
  agents-check` passes and each persona file exists under `.claude/agents/`.
- Given a dispatch for a phase that names a persona, when the prompt is built, then that
  persona's instructions are used rather than the default runner's - check: a test asserts
  the phase-to-role mapping resolves and the dispatch carries the role.
- Given a persona whose artifact does not exist, when it is proposed, then it is refused by
  D5's admission test - check: a test asserts a persona differing in neither tier, tools
  nor artifact cannot be registered.

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly loop run <feature>` at DECOMPOSE dispatches Dana with the decomposer's own
instructions, and `uv run basicly usage --json` attributes the spend to that role.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/agents/**`
- `.basicly/core/skills/**`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/agents.py`
- `tests/test_agents.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `140000`
- depends on: none

payload.text:
Scope sharpened by the owner 2026-08-08; requirements/factory-loop.md section 6 was rewritten to match and is now the spec.

Three things this bead must honour that its description understated:

1. NAMED FOR THE ROLE, NOT THE PERSONA. The catalog source is .basicly/core/agents/<role>/agent.yaml where <role> is decomposer, implementer, validator, reviewer, decider, retrospector, curator - the same vocabulary the state table in section 3.1 uses. Dana/Kai/Vera/Remo/Juno/Lumi/Tala are display-only and carry no authority; the engine keys on the role id, which is the directory name.

2. TWO CLASSES, and only one is bound to a state:
   - loop agents: dispatched by the engine at a state boundary, bound to exactly one state (two for the implementer's repair mode). All seven are missing.
   - ad-hoc agents: invoked on demand, bound to nothing, the same relationship skills already have. The three that exist - code-reviewer, security-auditor, test-runner - are ALL ad-hoc.
   A missing loop agent means that state has no specialist and falls back to the default runner. A missing ad-hoc agent costs only its own convenience.

3. THE THREE EXISTING AGENTS NEED EVALUATING, NOT ASSUMING. Each must still pass D5's admission test (differ in tier, tools or artifact), and any overlap with a loop agent about to be authored must be resolved rather than left as two things with one job: code-reviewer against reviewer, test-runner against the deterministic verify gates.

AND THE HALF THAT IS NOT AUTHORING. Measured 2026-08-08: the projection works and nothing consumes it. .claude/agents/ is written by agents.sync() and NO dispatch-path code reads an agent root; the only other consumer is cli.py:1261, which globs the directory to DELETE files. Every dispatch ends at Popen of a CLI with a prompt built inline. So authoring the sources is necessary and not sufficient - the engine must also resolve a state to a role and dispatch it. Splitting that into its own child is likely the right call at decompose.

## Context

`tests/test_tracker_requirements.py:392` — `test_r9_a_publish_that_would_shrink_the_export_is_refused_not_silent` — defines its own `publish` stand-in inside its body and asserts against that. It measures nothing about the product.

Its own docstring says so, and names the condition for repointing it:

> Written against a local helper rather than the replacement's API, which does not exist yet: this pins the *rule* so the replacement inherits it as a gate rather than as prose. **When the owned tracker lands, point this at its publish path.**

The owned tracker has landed. `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/snapshot.py` holds `write_snapshot`, `shrinkage` and `allow_shrink`, and `tests/test_kit_tracker_snapshot.py` exercises them — the release record `basicly-b2n2` bound its R9 claims to exactly those tests. So the instruction is due and the test still measures its own helper.

## Measured

```text
tests/test_tracker_requirements.py:412
    def publish(existing: Path, records: list[str], *, intent: bool = False) -> None:
        """Stand-in for the replacement's publish: refuse a silent shrink."""
```

The requirement register reports this row green, so the completeness gate reads a test that asserts its own fixture as coverage of R9.

## Why it is two changes, not one

Repointing this test fixes one row. **Nothing stops the next one**: a register row whose named test defines its own subject is invisible to every gate the repo has. The second half is the check that makes the class detectable, which is what the `curator` asked for.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN the R9 requirement test runs, IT SHALL exercise `snapshot.write_snapshot` and not a helper defined in its own body.
- WHEN a register row names a test, A CHECK SHALL refuse the row where that test defines its own subject, so a test measuring nothing cannot report green.
- WHERE such a row exists today, THE CHECK SHALL name every one rather than the first.

## Scope

- `tests/test_tracker_requirements.py`
- `.scripts/` (the register completeness check)

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: Break `snapshot.write_snapshot`'s shrink refusal and watch the R9 test go red, having first confirmed it stays green against the broken code today.

payload.description:
## Context

Tier 1 of basicly-ze8z: deterministic, so the engine should assert it rather than an operator remember it.

Three concrete items, each currently memory-only or memory-assisted:

- **FORCE_COLOR** - when set, it breaks the piped-output test and fails pre-push on an otherwise clean tree. **Zero mentions anywhere in the repo**: this is pure operator memory. `basicly loop preflight` or `basicly status` should report it, and the test that cares should be hermetic against it.
- **Node resolution in non-interactive shells** - on WSL, `npx` resolves to a Windows node in a non-interactive shell, so the markdownlint hook picks the wrong binary. The `node` skill documents the workaround; the hook should resolve its own interpreter instead, the way basicly-dukb made the Claude hook resolve its own script path.
- **The out-of-loop export scrub** - every `br` write re-adds `source_repo_path` to every record on re-export. Loop landings scrub automatically; a direct `br` write does not, so an operator must remember to call `basicly.br.scrub_export` before staging `.beads/`. Make the write path scrub, or make the pre-commit gate do it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an environment carrying any of these hazards when a run or a commit is attempted then the engine reports or corrects it, and no step requires an operator to have learned it first
payload.title: Make the out-of-loop tracker export scrub automatic

payload.text:
[harness-info] CORRECTION, 2026-08-01, owner-prompted. Two of the three items on this bead were
filed from unverified operator memory and one of them is not a real hazard. Measured on this machine
immediately after filing:

- `FORCE_COLOR` is **UNSET**, and was never set or unset by any command in the session that filed
  this bead. It appeared only in an operator's notes. **Drop it** unless someone can produce the
  failing run: the note claims it fails the piped-output test and pre-push, but nothing here
  reproduces that, and building an assertion for an unreproduced hazard is cost without evidence.
  If it is worth anything it is a hermetic-test question (the test should not care what the
  environment sets), not a preflight check.
- **Node resolution needs no workaround here either.** `which node npx` resolves to
  `<redacted:posix-home-path>,npx}` (v24.18.0) with **no PATH manipulation**, and
  `npx --yes markdownlint-cli2` runs clean without it. The operator had been prepending an nvm path
  to every commit for nothing - doubly so, because shell env does not persist between tool calls, so
  the export never reached the next command anyway. The original WSL observation may still hold on a
  machine with no local node install, so this needs a *reproduction on such a machine* before any
  code is written, not a note repeated.

What survives, and it is the only item with evidence behind it: **the out-of-loop export scrub.**
Every `br` write re-adds `source_repo_path` to every record on re-export; loop landings scrub
automatically, a direct write does not, and the operator remembers. That one is reproducible on
demand and is worth making automatic.

The general lesson, which is the point of the parent epic: an operator note is a *hypothesis about
the environment*. Externalizing it unmeasured just moves an unverified claim from memory into code,
where it costs a gate and a test to maintain. Measure first, then externalize what survives - see
[[closed-blocker-is-not-a-working-gate]] for the same error made against a closed bead.

payload.description: Discovered 2026-07-20 landing basicly-5wpn through the harness loop. At the build->verify landing advance, the engine committed accumulated base .beads dirt directly to base main (a chore(beads) sync commit), then rebased the harness branch onto the new base. The harness branch carries its own tracked .beads/issues.jsonl snapshot (from the provisioning claim commit) of the SAME bead the base commit just rewrote, so the rebase hits a one-line conflict on that issue in issues.jsonl. It recurs every rework attempt (each landing re-flushes the mutated DB, producing a new divergent line) and escalated at the rework cap, leaving TWO redundant chore(beads) commits on main plus a dirty base tree and the code stranded uncommitted in the worktree. Matches the beads-tracker-vs-loop-worktrees hazard (never commit issues.jsonl on a harness branch). Repro: claim+classify a leaf task, let provisioning leave base .beads dirty, run loop advance to land. Fix direction: before rebasing the harness branch, reset/checkout the branch's .beads/issues.jsonl to base (or exclude it from the branch entirely so only the redirect-shared DB carries tracker state), and ensure base .beads is committed cleanly before the rebase rather than mid-landing. Recovered 5wpn via the sanctioned base-checkout path.

payload.text: Root-cause correction (my original description was wrong). Reproduced with real git: the failure was NOT an issues.jsonl merge conflict. The agent's work was never committed on the harness branch, so merge_worktree's git rebase aborted with 'cannot rebase: you have unstaged changes' — a non-zero exit that line 185 misclassified as 'rebase-conflicts'. With the work committed, rebasing onto a tracker-advanced base succeeds cleanly (the code commit does not touch .beads, and base already carries the advanced tracker line). Confirmed CASE A (dirty->abort) vs CASE B (committed->clean rebase). Two real defects fixed: (1) no worktree-readiness precondition before rebasing; (2) an operator-fixable state burned rework and escalated with a misleading message. Fix: _worktree_land_readiness bails before touching base with a clear 'commit the work on <branch>' message when the tree is dirty or the branch has no commits ahead; _verify_and_land and merge_queue treat 'not-ready' as a plain block, not a rework attempt. Verified against real git for dirty/committed/empty/untracked-only cases; new regression tests in test_merge.py; harness-loop skill now tells the operator to commit on the branch before advancing.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the skill eval harness when it runs then it reports per-skill trigger accuracy and behavioral lift as an actionable pass-fail report a deliberately removed skill is caught and the case format plus how to add one per skill is documented with the full gate suite green
payload.description:
We distribute a catalog of skills (core + technology-scoped) but have NO evidence any of them actually do their job: whether a skill reliably TRIGGERS on the situations its description claims, and whether loading it measurably IMPROVES the agent's output vs not having it. Without evals we cannot tell a working skill from dead weight, catch a regression when a skill is edited, or justify what ships in the always-on baseline.

Goal: add an eval harness plus per-skill eval cases that measure (a) trigger accuracy (does the skill fire when it should and stay quiet when it should not) and (b) behavioral lift (does the guidance change the outcome on representative tasks). Reference approach to adapt: https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills/tree/main/evals (eval cases per skill run against a model).

Scope to decide when picked up: eval file format and where cases live in the catalog; a basicly command to run them (and optionally a CI gate); which skills get cases first (start with the core universal skills and the highest-value tech skills); how to score trigger vs lift; cost/model controls so the suite is affordable to run.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An eval harness exists and is documented; at least the core universal skills have eval cases covering trigger accuracy and behavioral lift.
- Running the evals produces a pass/fail (or scored) report a human can act on; a deliberately broken/removed skill is caught.
- The format and how to add a case per skill are documented (catalog-authoring or a dedicated doc). Full gate suite passes.
payload.title: Skill evals: prove distributed skills actually change agent behavior

payload.text: Integrated into docs/factory-design.md as component 11 and section 8: regression gate for the factory prose surfaces (lane runbook, agent-client skill, decider guidance); no prerequisite; will be linked into the factory implementation epic.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane escalated at its rework cap when a human answers the escalation with a retry then exactly one further attempt is permitted for that gate on that node without changing the repo-wide cap and with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Found in the basicly-kjc5.22 dogfood run (feature basicly-hxnf, 2026-07-26).

Lane `basicly-hxnf.1` hit the merge rework cap, so the supervisor escalated it to the decision
queue asking "retry, re-dispatch, or park?". The operator answered `retry` with evidence that the
gate failure was not the lane's work. **The answer cannot be carried out.**

`policy.record_rework` only ever increments and `policy.rework_attempts` only reads; there is no
clear, reset, or decrement anywhere, and `basicly policy rework` exposes only `--record`. So the
counter stays at the cap, and the next landing attempt escalates again immediately. The queue item
is answered but the lane cannot move.

The operator's only levers are both wrong: raise `[policy] max_rework` in config, which loosens
the cap for *every* node in the repo, or land the lane by hand, which is exactly what
basicly-kjc5.22's acceptance criterion forbids. The escalation therefore offers three choices and
implements none of them.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Let a lane fail its landing gate until `rework: N/N attempts - ESCALATE (cap reached)`.
2. `basicly loop answer <decision-id> "retry"` — succeeds.
3. `basicly loop advance <lane>` — blocks and re-escalates at once; `basicly policy rework <lane> --gate merge` still reports the cap.
4. Expected: an answered `retry` lets exactly one further attempt through, without changing the repo-wide cap.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane escalated at its rework cap when a human answers the escalation with a retry then exactly one further attempt is permitted for that gate on that node without changing the repo-wide cap and with tests

## Scope

- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `src/basicly/decisions.py`
payload.title: An answered retry escalation cannot be acted on because nothing clears the rework counter

When a commit message or a tag message mentions -c core.hooksPath or --no-verify, I want the deny-list to admit the commit, so I can document the bypass fix without a deny from prose.

1. Install basicly v0.19.2 and run basicly permissions-build.

payload.description:
## CORRECTED 2026-08-13 — read this before the text below
The routing defect is exactly true: `resolve_role` still has **one** call site, `loop.py:745`
inside `_run_agent`, whose three call sites are `build`, `repair` and `build`. **The
reproduction, the remedy and the ranking below are all wrong.**

**Classify and decompose do dispatch today, through a function this bead does not mention.**
`loop.py:1002-1051 _run_proposer` calls `runner.run(...)` at `:1033` with **no `role=`
kwarg**, reached from `_on_intake` and `_on_classify` under an L2+ grant. It landed in
`a983785` on 2026-08-07 - **two days before this bead was written**. So the block message
quoted in Steps to Reproduce is real but misattributed: it is `_proposal_declined`'s fallback,
and the engine was not unable to call a decomposer. Why it declined on 2026-08-09 was never
recorded and the quote is truncated before the reason.

**The remedy shape would lose three things.** Acceptance criterion 1 says dispatch through
`_run_agent` with `phase='classify'`. That discards `runner.confine_for_decider`
(`loop.py:1026`, the tool confinement that bounds a proposer to its own requirement), the
reserved `runner.DECIDER` process slot, and the `PROPOSE_PHASE` run-record classification that
keeps proposals out of the write-dispatch calibration sample. **The correct minimal change is
one `role=roles.resolve_role(...)` argument at `loop.py:1033`, plus the same at
`supervise.py:2669`** - the lane path passes no role at all today (`rg role
src/basicly/supervise.py` returns zero hits).

**The headline number is optimistic.** Not "1 of 7": **0 of 346 recorded dispatch commands
contain `--agent`**, against a positive control of 163 containing `-p`. `implementer` is
reachable by code reading and has never been *observed* on an argv.

**The ranking argument is weakened.** The claim that `u6jq.1` cannot pass while this is open
rests on every decomposition being hand-dispatched; `_run_proposer` removes the human from that
boundary under a grant. What remains is that the proposal runs **without the decomposer
persona**. And because `--agent` does not preload `skills:` (`basicly-ey58`), this remedy
delivers a role's system prompt, tools and model but not the `decompose-plan` skill it
declares - so its ceiling is lower than assumed.

This is also the seam `basicly-u2hl.54.3` needs; do that one after this.

---

Measured 2026-08-09 in base @ 5132143, while decomposing basicly-u2hl.54.

basicly-4kdm closed 2026-08-08 claiming both halves - definitions and dispatch. The dispatch
half reaches exactly one role.

  resolve_role is called from ONE place:  loop.py:745, inside _run_agent
  _run_agent has three call sites:
    loop.py:594   _run_agent(ctx, ctx.issue_id, cwd)          phase='build'  -> implementer
    loop.py:1642  _run_agent(..., phase='repair')             phase='repair' -> implementer
    loop.py:1758  _run_agent(ctx, subtask_id, cwd)            phase='build'  -> implementer

_run_agent signature is (ctx, issue_id, cwd, *, prompt=None, phase='build') at loop.py:709.
classify and decompose never call _run_agent at all, so decider and decomposer cannot reach an
argv through the engine no matter what ROLE_BY_PHASE says.

So the standing claim 'only 3 of 7 loop roles can ever be invoked - classify, decompose,
build/repair' is wrong. It is 1 of 7 - implementer - reached through 2 phases that map to the
same role. The other six are definitions with no caller.

Demonstrated the hard way: the decomposition for basicly-u2hl.54 was produced by dispatching
the decomposer agent BY HAND from the driving session, because `basicly loop advance` at the
decompose boundary reports 'decompose needs an agent-proposed child plan' and blocks. The
engine has the role, the agent file and the skill, and still cannot call it.

This is the recurring shape: a closed bead proves code exists, not that the path binds.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When the engine needs a work type at intake or classify, it shall dispatch through
  `_run_agent` with `phase='classify'` so `roles.resolve_role` places `--agent decider` on
  the runner argv, under a covering grant, instead of blocking for an agent-proposed value.
- When the engine needs a child plan at decompose, it shall dispatch through `_run_agent` with
  `phase='decompose'` so `roles.resolve_role` places `--agent decomposer` on the argv.
- Where the selected runner family cannot load the role from its projected agent root, the
  engine shall dispatch the default runner rather than emit a flag the host silently drops.
- Where no covering grant exists, the engine shall block for a human exactly as it does today,
  so this changes who is dispatched and not what may be self-approved.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/roles.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`
- `tests/test_roles.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`
- `changelog.d/basicly-4xmu.fixed.md`

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `uv run basicly loop advance <feature-id>` at the decompose boundary.
2. It blocks with 'decompose needs an agent-proposed child plan'.
3. `rg -n 'resolve_role' src/basicly/` returns one call site, inside `_run_agent`.
4. `rg -n '_run_agent\(' src/basicly/loop.py` returns three call sites, none for classify or
   decompose.
payload.title: Route the classify and decompose dispatches through resolve_role

payload.text:
Ranked ABOVE basicly-u2hl.54.1 by the owner, 2026-08-09.

Reason: until classify and decompose reach resolve_role, every decomposition is hand-dispatched
from a driving session. That happened for real on basicly-u2hl.54 this session - the plan was
produced by invoking the decomposer agent by hand because `loop advance` blocks at the decompose
boundary asking for a plan it cannot request.

The consequence is not just inconvenience: basicly-u6jq.1 is the proof that a supervised pass
completes with zero interventions attributable to a harness defect. A boundary that always needs
a human to fetch an agent the engine already owns is such a defect, so u6jq.1 cannot pass while
this is open.

Cost argues the same way. u2hl.54.1 forecasts 48M tokens; this is a routing change across
loop.py and roles.py with no phase-tuple insertion behind it.

Still behind rrah and 5vu4, which are P0 data-loss.

payload.description:
## Context
When the owner corrected the tracker requirements on 2026-11-12 (any git host, no provider or gh, nothing to set up, a flat file count, no push rights on main, 3 to 9 people with about 200 pull requests a day), I want to grade four storage shapes against those properties in a short hill-climb, so the owner can pick a winner before more vault work is built. Candidates: A vault repository as built, B a dedicated tracker branch with the same per-writer files and claim code, C events that travel with the work branches, D a server such as Dolt. Time box 2 hours, at most 2 rounds, no product code; a spike in a scratch folder is allowed.
payload.title: Pick a tracker storage shape for the corrected owner requirements

payload.text: Brief from the orchestrator for the owner, 2026-11-12. Fixed properties, graded 0 to 10: P1 git only, any host, no provider API or gh. P2 setup: commands, repositories, tokens and chores a team needs; zero is the target. P3 file count stays flat with pull requests, branches, records and events; 200 pull requests a day is 2,000 in 10 days. P4 no pull request ever conflicts on tracker data. P5 no push rights on main needed. P6 load: 3 to 9 people, about 200 pull requests a day with AI. P7 a claim is known within seconds; no record with two holders. P8 in sync with the code. P9 nothing hidden: ordinary tools show the data, and a person can find and remove it. P10 clone size and noise on the code repository after one year. Tie-breaker only: how much of today's built code stays. Candidates: A vault repository in its best form (one command, registry optional); B one dedicated tracker branch with per-writer files and the built share and claim code (the owner banned an orphan branch on 2026-11-11 under nothing hidden; grade P9 on what each host shows); C events travel with the work branches, reads fold main plus every remote branch, branch name is the claim, a routine pull request compacts (grade with and without compaction); D a server such as Dolt. At most one candidate E if a grader finds a shape that beats these on P2 and P3 together. Method: hill-climb with fresh graders per round, at most 2 rounds, only the top two improve between rounds, a fresh verifier runs falsify-first and one spike on the leader; for B the spike runs the built share and claim code on a branch of a local bare repository, runs T-share-smoke and the claim proofs, and measures repository size after one simulated year and what a default and a single-branch clone fetch; interface-facts for GitHub and Bitbucket on CI for a branch with no pipeline file and branch rules that exempt one branch. A council votes if two candidates end within one grade point. Time box 2 hours, no product code.

Climb result 2026-11-12, 2 rounds, 8 graders, 1 verifier with a spike, council of 3. Round 1 sums of lowest grades: A 69, B 59, C 57, C+ 58, D 59, E 74 (E = B made readable). Round 2: A2 65, E2 59 (means 7.5 and 7.3). Council A2 3 to 0, voted before the verifier reported. Verifier: 'A2 reads from a shallow clone' broke (a depth-1 clone folds 0 holders and a claim from it landed on a held record; the built code never makes a shallow clone, so this blocks a proposed shortcut, not today's code); 'A2 setup is one command' broke (git cannot create a host repository; 5 to 6 host steps plus one invitation per member; no init verb); 'never two holders with full history' held (117 proof tests passed). Full-history cost in the built log format: 1.31 KiB per commit marginal (measured), about 270 MiB per year and about 38 minutes of first fold per year (extrapolated); shared by any shape that uses the built log and fold. Verdict: A, the vault repository in its BUILT log form; v2's state files, generation floor, create-on-init and .git/ local copy are dropped. Not a clean win: E2 beats A2 on P1 (8 against 6) and P2 (7 against 4); A leads on P10 and P5. No candidate meets both the 2026-11-11 rulings as relayed (no tracker branch, git refs banned, the separate backlog repository stands) and the 2026-11-12 correction as relayed (a second repository is too heavy). Owner decisions: (1) keep a second repository with a manual host step, or lift the branch ban and accept that a default code clone carries the tracker history (measured 71 to 491 MiB in one simulated year, on the rejected state-file format); recommend the repository; (2) the claim protocol stays; (3) history growth stands until a checkpoint design exists. D (a server) scored 59 with P1 at 0 to 2. Estimate, assumed: 8 to 12 slices, 2 to 3 weeks, plus 1 to 2 weeks for the unscoped checkpoint design.

Owner decision 2026-11-12, relayed by the orchestrator: (1) the owner agrees to the vault repository design (candidate A as built); the name is open and sets the default repository name at init; the orchestrator recommends 'the vault' with default repository name backlog-vault. (2) Migration must not lose existing backlogs: basicly ledger files (events-*.jsonl, pending-*.jsonl, snapshot.jsonl) and br/beads issues.jsonl or similar JSON or JSONL trackers; ids are kept. (3) Requirements in the owner's words: 'basicly tracker can be installed as standalone and as part of basicly harness'; 'basicly tracker can be used with other harnesses and can hook into them (example with scripts, skills, cli, api, and so on)'; 'we do not need any secrets, tokens or similar' - the vault uses the person's own git credentials; the CI testbed token, the two repository variables and the testbed-probe job are dropped from .43.25. (4) Dogfood cutover approved in order basicly, handily, terminal, each after the one before works (ledger lines measured by the orchestrator: basicly 19150, handily 4194, terminal 2096; all three code repositories public). (5) Open owner question: one vault for many projects or one per project. The hold on vault slices ends; nothing is built before the plan is sent to the orchestrator.

Finding from basicly-af8bh74, 2026-11-12: a tracker branch in the code repository can bound its clone cost only with a period branch restarted at each checkpoint (measured: 1.36 MiB of tracker objects in a default clone against 97.7 MiB for the full branch after one simulated year). The old periods must then live under a custom ref such as refs/tracker-archive/*, which is the hidden git-ref storage the owner banned; under a tag they return into every default clone; with no ref git gc deletes them. So the branch shape bounds its cost only by hiding or losing the archive. This settles the question for the vault repository.

payload.description:
When an upgrade runs in a repository that has no CI workflow, I want to know whether creating one is something install may do without being asked, so I can stop a tool writing into a directory a consumer never opted into.

Found by the terminal canary as term-42xuc arm 1, confirmed here at cli.py:1239-1241: the branch that runs when the path does not exist calls mkdir and write and prints Wrote, and it never consults force. So --overwrite-scaffolds is not what arms creation; a plain install is. I reproduced it by accident in this repository, which had never tracked .github/workflows/basicly-gates.yml and had one after a mistaken install.

Re-pinning a file a consumer already has is a different act from creating one they never had, and the second is the larger one. This is filed apart from basicly-kfj94k8, which only removes the backup inversion, because the answer here is a decision rather than a defect.

The canary listed four shapes without prescribing one: announce before writing, back up on the re-pin path, gate creation behind an explicit opt-in, or add install --dry-run. The second is done. The remaining three are alternatives, not a sequence.
payload.requirements: the decision is written where the other fifty are rather than in a changelog entry. No behaviour changes until it is taken, because the current behaviour is documented in the file's own first line and changing it silently is the same class of surprise being complained about.
payload.title: decide whether a plain install may create a ci workflow unasked

payload.text: [research findings 2026-10-31] Recommendation: make creation of a new CI workflow opt-in. A fresh-repository install from the published v0.35.1 wheel actually created .github/workflows/basicly-gates.yml. Current src/basicly/cli.py _scaffold_repo calls _scaffold_consumer_files, which unconditionally calls _scaffold_ci_workflow; _write_scaffold creates an absent file. Existing workflows can also have basicly pins/runtime updated with a backup, so the generated header's never-overwrites wording is not the full upgrade contract. The workflow subscribes to push/pull_request on main and workflow_dispatch, uses contents:read, and runs harness full verification. Inference: default creation can activate unexpected remote work/policy on the next push and can imply application checks that a new basicly.toml has not configured. Staying default favors immediate enforcement but has that surprise failure mode. Announce-then-write keeps immediate enforcement but a noninteractive install can bury the warning before the same surprise. Opt-in avoids unsolicited automation but leaves remote enforcement absent when the operator misses setup; counter it with a clear next command and an explicit CI-status message. Existing user-owned workflows must remain preserved, and any pin/runtime update contract must be separately explicit. Exactly left: owner acceptance of this decision, an authorized implementation of opt-in workflow creation and a regression asserting plain install does not create a new workflow while explicit opt-in does. No CI/scaffold behavior was changed during this research; the record's enforcement criterion is not yet met. GitHub's event trigger contract is documented at https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/trigger-a-workflow.

[research handover] Recommendation remains opt-in creation of new CI workflows. The earlier comment records the observed default write and the failure modes of default, opt-in and announce-then-write. Exact remaining work: full research review/check plan, acceptance of the policy decision, separately authorized implementation of that decision, and the criterion's regression proving plain install cannot create a new workflow under the opt-in rule while explicit opt-in can. Preserve consumer-owned existing workflow content and make any pin/runtime update contract explicit. No CI or scaffold behavior was changed during this evaluation.

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a repository adopts the work tracker through `basicly install` its ledger gets no union-merge attribute, so two branches that each append an event conflict, and the promise the tracker exists to make is not delivered on the path most consumers take.

## Steps to Reproduce

Measured 2026-09-12 in a throwaway git repository with a real `basicly install`.

```
$ basicly install
basicly install complete: repo converged.
$ ls .gitattributes
".gitattributes": No such file or directory
$ git check-attr text merge -- .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl
.basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl: text: unspecified
.basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl: merge: unspecified
```

The control, the same probe against a standalone `basicly-tracker init`:

```
tracker: added to .gitattributes: events-*.jsonl -text merge=union
$ git check-attr text merge -- .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl
.basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl: text: unset
.basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl: merge: union
```

So the standalone installer is **more correct than the integrated one**, which is the wrong way round.

## Why no gate caught it

`grep -rn 'gitattributes|merge=union|check-attr' src/basicly/*.py .basicly/core/hooks/*.py` returns nothing. Positive control: the same grep for `gitignore` returns 10 files, so the probe discriminates. Repo-wide, `merge=union` appears in six files and exactly one of them **writes** it - `packages/basicly-tracker/basicly_tracker/__init__.py`, built 2026-09-12. `.scripts/kit_deployment.py` only checks it, and `.scripts/` does not ship to a consumer, so a consumer has neither the write nor the check.

basicly-aabirfj closed by declaring the attribute in **this repository's own hand-written `.gitattributes`** and gating it here. Its last acceptance criterion - "THE KIT SHALL install this attribute into a consumer repository" - was explicitly discharged to basicly-ssbkq5c, which built the standalone installer only. Nothing carried it into `basicly install`. The criterion was met for one of the two ways in.

## Blast radius

Every consumer that adopted the tracker through `basicly install`. The failure is silent until two branches append, and then it is a content conflict in a large JSONL file that a human must hand-resolve - the exact failure the append-only design exists to remove.

## Acceptance Criteria

- THE INSTALL SHALL write every git attribute and ignore rule the tracker kit's correctness depends on, reading the globs off `events.LOG_GLOB` and `snapshot.DERIVED_PATTERNS` rather than spelling them again.
- THE INSTALL SHALL refuse rather than converge where it cannot write them, matching the standalone installer.
- THE INSTALL SHALL be idempotent, and SHALL NOT disturb a rule the consumer already wrote.
- A CHECK THAT SHIPS TO THE CONSUMER SHALL report a ledger whose attribute is absent, since `.scripts/kit_deployment.py` does not travel.
- A TEST SHALL install into a throwaway repository and assert `git check-attr` reports `text: unset` and `merge: union`, with a control asserting the same history conflicts without them.
- THE TWO INSTALL PATHS SHALL agree, and a test SHALL assert that what `basicly install` guarantees for the tracker is what `basicly-tracker init` guarantees.

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- demonstration: install through basicly into a throwaway repo, build two branches that each append an event, merge them, and read every event present afterwards
payload.title: basicly install leaves the ledger without the union merge attribute

Proved in a fresh repo: git check-attr reports text unset and merge union. The merge control now discriminates, which the first one did not - no attribute conflicts, -text alone conflicts, -text merge=union merges clean with all three events. Nine tests including both negative controls, and one asserting the two install paths carry the same rule. The helper sits behind the write seam because test_gate_source refused a direct owned_store.kit call from cli.py, which is the boundary working.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane whose verify gate fails on a check that passes when re-run unchanged when the landing is triaged then the failure is distinguished from a merit failure and does not consume the lane's rework budget with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Found in the basicly-kjc5.22 dogfood run (feature basicly-hxnf, 2026-07-26).

Lane `basicly-hxnf.1`'s landing failed its `verify full` gate on
`tests/test_integration_loop.py::test_landing_blocks_instead_of_reworking_an_uncommitted_worktree`,
which failed with the known `br` clock defect (`updated_at: cannot be before created_at`). The
lane's own commit was three documentation files under `.basicly/core/skills/python/` and its two
projections — it cannot affect that test. Re-running the test in the lane's own worktree
immediately afterwards: 1 fail, 2 passes, no change in between.

The harness charged the lane a rework attempt for it, reached the cap, and escalated it to a human.
So a pre-existing upstream flake is scored exactly like a merit failure, and it cost the run its
acceptance criterion — two of three lanes landed unattended, the third was escalated for something
it did not do.

This is the harness-side half of the tracker defect that `basicly-vkh0` exists to remove; filing it
separately because the fix is different. `vkh0` stops the flake existing. This bead is about the
engine having no way to tell "the gate is unreliable" from "the work is wrong", so a flake silently
consumes a lane's bounded rework budget.

Design note: `basicly-kjc5.52` (fingerprint the environment behind a gate result) is adjacent — a
gate result that carries provenance is what would let a re-run be compared rather than merely
repeated.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Land a lane whose verify suite contains a test that fails intermittently for reasons unrelated to the lane's diff.
2. Observe `routed: <lane> -> decision - merge failed: verify full failed: pytest (rework 1/1)`.
3. Re-run the failing test unchanged — it passes.
4. Expected: a gate failure that does not reproduce is not charged against the lane's rework budget.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane whose verify gate fails on a check that passes when re-run unchanged when the landing is triaged then the failure is distinguished from a merit failure and does not consume the lane's rework budget with tests

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
payload.title: A flaky gate consumes a lane's rework budget as if the work were wrong

payload.text: [harness-policy] checkpoint=classify approved

[harness-run] id=basicly-55yh#run-4bede34c79 phase=build
{"agent": "manual", "outcome": "handoff", "phase": "build", "prompt_sha256": "f62813cc661f9fce86e98c5b4261431363e0b3ee3f950cafa895b3ba11da0ebe", "scope_tokens": 26900, "timestamp": "2026-07-26T14:26:06.311547+00:00"}
[harness-policy] checkpoint=ship approved

Flake observed 2026-07-27 during the basicly-m4zv.9 build, in the worktree, on 'basicly verify --mode full': one run reported '1 failed, 1460 passed'. Seven subsequent runs of the same command in the same tree were clean (2x verify --mode full at 1461 passed, 5x pytest -q -n auto at 1461 passed), so roughly 1 in 8.

The test name is UNKNOWN and that is my process error, not a property of the flake: I piped the failing run through 'tail -12', which showed the summary block and discarded the FAILED line above it. Anyone chasing this should redirect the whole run to a file first.

Signal worth keeping: the gate's pytest check runs 'pytest -q -n auto' (basicly.toml line 92) while a bare 'uv run pytest -q' is serial and took 49s against the parallel 11s. So the flake is most likely xdist worker- or order-dependent rather than time-dependent, which narrows where to look - shared filesystem or global state between tests that land on different workers.

This is exactly the cost 55yh describes: had it hit during the landing advance instead of a hand-run, it would have spent one of the lane's two rework attempts on nothing.

IDENTIFIED, same session: the flake reproduced on the basicly-m4zv.9 landing advance and it is the known upstream br clock defect, not a new one.

  FAILED tests/test_integration_loop.py::test_the_engine_commits_the_claim_before_provisioning
  RuntimeError: br update <id> --external-ref worktree:<id>:harness/<id> failed:
    Error: Validation failed: updated_at: cannot be before created_at

So the signature is the same 'updated_at cannot be before created_at' one already carried as a requirement on the Phase 6 replacement per plan section 3 principle 6. The earlier note in this thread guessed xdist worker or order dependence; that was wrong. It is a clock-resolution artifact in br's own validation when a create and an update land inside the same tick, which is why parallel runs make it more likely without being the cause.

Cost, measured rather than argued: it charged 'rework 1/2' against basicly-m4zv.9 for a defect in a dependency, with nothing in our tree to fix. That is precisely the waste this bead exists to stop, and it is now a concrete instance rather than a prediction. Nothing in the m4zv.9 diff touches the loop, br, or that test.

payload.description:
## Context

Observed on `basicly-gvlpxm` on 2026-08-20, and it is why that lane could not be closed by
advancing it.

The lane sat at phase `validate` with `validate-as-consumer` failed and rework 1 of 2. Its worktree
still held `.basicly/usage/repair-brief.json`, and that brief names the defect *recording the post
regeneration branch head*. **That defect was fixed and landed hours earlier** by a hand repair in the
same worktree, which became `merge.MergeResult.landed_head`. The brief has `findings: []` and
`evidence: []`; it carries only the two clipped reviews.

So `_repair_in_place` would have found the brief and **dispatched a full metered repair for work that is
done**. Nothing invalidates a brief when its defect is closed by another route - not the landing that
carried the fix, not the gate, and not the brief's own reader.

**The second half is the wedge, and it is why this is not merely wasteful.** A repair that finds nothing
to do commits nothing, so the branch carries nothing base does not hold, so the next advance takes the
same branch again. If the brief is consumed on read the following advance falls through to `_rework` and
charges the last slot for a round with nothing wrong in it. Either way the record cannot leave `validate`,
and its work is already in main and independently green.

I predicted the fall-through and was wrong: I assumed the brief had been consumed by the hand repair. It
had not. **Probe for the brief file rather than reasoning about whether it was taken.**

Related and visible in the same artifact: the reviews in this brief are clipped with a leading
`(earlier output cut)`, so the defect statement is what the clip dropped. That is `basicly-jr0l.74`,
still live.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take a record at phase validate whose gate failed and whose worktree holds a repair brief.
2. Fix the named defect by any route other than a briefed repair - a hand fix, or a sibling lane - and land it.
3. Observe the brief file is still present and still names the fixed defect.
4. Run `basicly loop advance <id>` and observe it dispatch a repair rather than refuse the stale brief.
5. Observe the repair has nothing to commit, so the branch carries nothing unlanded and the next advance reaches the same state.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a repair brief whose named defect is already landed when the lane advances then the brief is refused as stale rather than dispatched - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_repair_brief.py -k stale -q`
- Given a repair that commits nothing when the advance completes then the lane is blocked naming that fact rather than charging rework or re-dispatching the same brief
- Given a brief whose defect is still open then it is dispatched unchanged

## Scope

- `src/basicly/repair_brief.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_repair_brief.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/repair_brief.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_repair_brief.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest -q`
payload.title: a repair brief outlives the defect it names so a lane is driven to repair work already landed

payload.text:
The signal needed no clock. A brief records the branch head it was written against, and a moved head means that work landed by another route - the only fact that changes when work lands. Both halves fail quiet on anything short of proof: a brief predating the field, and a ref that will not resolve. Refusing on the reader's own uncertainty would strand work a red gate really does owe.

Two mutations, each failing its own tests: never detecting staleness, and refusing on cannot-tell.

A LINTER DECIDED WHERE THE CODE WENT, and it was right. _repair_in_place sits at exactly ruff PLR0911's six-return budget - the same budget that forced _repair_outcome out of it under basicly-dbbh - so the staleness refusal WIDENS the existing early-out rather than adding a branch, and the committed-nothing check went into _repair_outcome, whose stated job is what a finished repair leaves the loop blocked on. Both messages live in repair_brief.py beside the predicate that raises them, and a landed=(branch, head) tuple collapsed to a branch name once I noticed the brief already records the head to compare against.

I wrote genuinely bad code fighting that budget under size pressure - an expression calling a function that does not exist - and restored loop.py rather than patching it, then reimplemented with the budget known up front.

loop.py took a 44-token rebaseline, its FIRST EVER: load_ratchet().rebaselined reports no prior entry, so this is not the accumulation basicly-wpqdag made visible. Second behavioural fix into that module today after basicly-3katht. Prose share FELL 52.4 to 52.3, which is the control that the 44 tokens are code and not comment.

Full verify PASS, 32 checks, 4542 tests.

Not done: the phase model question basicly-3katht raised is still open, and a stale brief is now refused rather than prevented - nothing invalidates a brief at the moment its defect closes, the refusal happens when the next advance reads it.
