payload.description:
## Problem

`_assert_interval` in `tests/test_integration_wait.py` guards only the upper side of the injected
wait offset. Its lower bound is bare:

```python
assert _WAITED_S <= waited_s <= _WAITED_S + elapsed_s + _SLACK_S
```

The meter computes `waited_s` as the harness clock (`policy._now`, monkeypatched to
`time.time() + 600`) minus the `created_at` that the **separate `br` process** stamped. The lower
bound therefore asserts that br's stamp never lands ahead of this process's `time.time()`. With
whole-second resolution across two processes under load, it can, and the interval reads one second
short.

The docstring already acknowledges the truncation ("the meter may read a second or two over") but
draws the conclusion in one direction only. basicly-o7z5 fixed the upper bound for the symmetric
reason - a loaded machine made two real br round-trips exceed a flat five-second slack. The lower
bound is the same defect class left in place.

This matters beyond a red suite: a flaky gate consumes a lane's rework budget as if the work were
wrong, which is exactly what basicly-55yh exists to prevent. A flake inside the `verify` gate is
therefore a factory-reliability defect, not merely a test annoyance.

## Steps to Reproduce

Observed on main at 7db0143 during `basicly verify --mode full`:

```
assert 600 <= 599
E       assert _WAITED_S <= waited_s <= _WAITED_S + elapsed_s + _SLACK_S
tests/test_integration_wait.py:59: AssertionError
FAILED tests/test_integration_wait.py::test_a_queued_decision_wait_round_trips_through_the_real_tracker
1 failed, 1997 passed in 40.39s
```

Load-dependent, so it does not reproduce in isolation:

- the same test alone, five consecutive runs: 5 passed, 0 failed
- `uv run pytest -q -n 4` immediately afterwards on the same tree: 1998 passed

## Context

Owner, reading the board 2026-09-05: *"i have no idea do we see what task are being worked on."*

They could not, and the page held the count three times over. Measured on the served document:

```text
THE LOOP    build 1
THE BACKLOG BUILD 1
BACKLOG     IN PROGRESS 1
RUNNING NOW (no cards)
```

Nine record ids are drawn on the page, all nine in `NEXT UP`, none of them the one in progress. A reader is told a record is being worked on three times and can never learn which.

## Why `RUNNING NOW` does not cover it

That region draws `lanes[]`, and a lane exists only where a supervised pass dispatched one. A record at `build` with no lane — picked up by hand, or a pass that ended without tearing down — is in progress by every count the page prints and absent from the only region that names work.

So this is not `basicly-9guj21`, which is about work the board *cannot* see. This is work the board **can** see, counts, and does not name.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a record is at a working phase with no lane, THE PAGE SHALL name it — its id, its title and its phase — and SHALL NOT report the count alone.
- WHEN such a record is drawn, IT SHALL be visually distinct from a dispatched lane, because it has no agent, no branch and no spend.
- WHEN a count on the page names a population of one or more, SOME REGION SHALL name at least one member of it, or the count SHALL say why it cannot.
- WHERE nothing is at a working phase, THE REGION SHALL collapse rather than reserve space.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_regions.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/board_page.html.j2`
- `tests/test_board_regions.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: Serve the board with one record at `build` and no lane, and read its id off the page.

## Context

Found by the 2026-07-31 session retro. Shipping `basicly-kjc5.58` under an active L3 grant on
`basicly-kjc5` demanded a confirm code, while two earlier beads the same session shipped with
`delegated under L3 grant`. The behaviour is CORRECT - `policy._grant_approval` requires
`lights_out_violations` to be empty for a ship, the preconditions are session-wide, and the measured
cause was `rework escalation on basicly-kjc5.56 (gate verify: 2/2)`, a wrinkle in a sibling bead
elsewhere in the epic's 55-issue session. D3 deliberately drops ship back to a human on any wrinkle.

The defect is that the refusal is **silent about why**. `_grant_approval` returns `None` and the
caller mints a confirm challenge, so the operator sees only `CONFIRMATION REQUIRED` with no
indication that a grant existed, covered the checkpoint, was not spend-halted, and was declined for a
specific reason in a different issue. Diagnosing it took several tool calls reading `policy.py` and
then calling `lights_out_violations` by hand.

This will recur on every child ship under any epic carrying an unresolved wrinkle, which for
`basicly-kjc5` is every remaining bead in the model-tier chain.

Related precedent for the fix's shape: the deterministic grant refusals in `_grant_refusal` already
return an explanatory string rather than a bare failure, so the module already has the idiom.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Have an active L3 grant on an epic root and a rework escalation on any child in that session.
- Run `basicly loop run <other-child> --root <epic>` to the ship checkpoint.
- Observed: `checkpoint ship: CONFIRMATION REQUIRED` with no reason, and nothing indicating a grant
  was present and declined. Expected: the output names the violated lights-out precondition and the
  issue it belongs to, so the operator can either fix it or knowingly relay the code.

payload.value:
## Context

Found 2026-08-20 while closing `basicly-z9xvwa` through the documented write surface. The
close landed and the reason did not.

`mirror._close_drafts` emits one `KIND_STATUS` draft and nothing else, so a `--reason` the
argv carries reaches the owned ledger as no event at all. Its docstring justifies the drop:
the reason is not mirrored **as a comment**, because br records it as a field of the close
and inventing a comment row would be a difference the mirror made rather than found. That
argument is correct and it is about the wrong shape. The kit already models the field —
`commands.CLOSE_REASON_FIELD`, written as a `KIND_FIELD` draft by `commands.close` — so
mirroring it as a field is exactly what makes the two sides identical.

`closed_at` is lost by the same route.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `basicly tracker write -- close <id> --reason "<text>"` on an open record.
2. Observe the surface print `recorded: close <id> --reason <text>`.
3. Run `basicly tracker show <id>` and observe `status` is `closed`, and that `close_reason` and `closed_at` are both absent.
4. Observe `max_seq` advanced by exactly **1**, so only the status event was appended - had the reason been carried it would be 2, because `commands.close` drafts the field before the status.
5. Positive control on the field itself: 663 of the 772 closed records in `.basicly/ledger/snapshot.jsonl` carry `close_reason`, so the field is the norm rather than an unused one, and the 0 above belongs to the write path and not to the fold.

## The population, split rather than counted

109 of the 772 closed records carry neither `close_reason` nor `closed_at`, and the record
closed above now matches that signature exactly. That is one signature, not a proven
attribution: a record closed before either field existed is indistinguishable from one closed
through this path. **Split the 109 against the first commit that introduced the field before
reporting any of them as this defect** - the count is a question, and only the part of it that
postdates the field is an answer.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a close carrying a reason through the write seam when the record is read back then the reason is on the record as a field - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_mirror.py -k close_reason -q`
- Given a close carrying no reason then exactly the events it carries today are appended, so no existing record's history changes meaning
- Given the 109 closed records with neither field then the record states how many postdate the field's introduction, measured rather than assumed

## Scope

- `src/basicly/mirror.py`
- `tests/test_mirror.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/mirror.py`
- `tests/test_mirror.py`
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/commands.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest -q`

payload.text:
Closed by 3e75b8e7, and THIS close is the demonstration: the reason landed as a field and max_seq moved by 2 rather than 1. Every close I made earlier in this session lost its reason to the defect being fixed here.

Third acceptance criterion, answered by measurement: 119 closed records carry no reason and NOT ONE predates the field. Dated each by the timestamp of its own status event against the earliest close that carries a reason - 2026-07-12T23:12:00 - and 0 fall before it. So all 119 are this defect, none is a record closed before the rule existed. The record said 109; the delta of 10 is this session's own closes going through the same seam.

The agreement the engine cannot reach at runtime is pinned from the test side: the kit module the mirror is handed is differential, which exposes events and migrate and not commands, so a test loads commands.py by path and asserts CLOSE_REASON_FIELD is equal. Same route labels.WRITER_LABELS takes.

An existing test asserted the OLD behaviour - _one(...) on a close with a reason. Its stated intent, that mirroring a comment would invent a difference, is still right and the fix honours it, so it became a two-draft assertion that also asserts neither draft is a comment. Then the duplicate of it in test_mirror.py was removed, which is what took that module back under its baseline.

Full verify PASS, 31 checks, 4511 tests.

Not done: 119 records still carry no reason and nothing backfills them. An append-only log cannot rewrite them, and a reason invented now would be a claim nobody made. They stay as the population this defect produced.

payload.description:
## Context

**A ratchet bounds a file. Nothing bounds the tree.**

Measured 2026-08-14: `src/basicly/` went from **36,641 lines to 42,966 in one week** - about +17% - with every structural gate live and green throughout:

```text
module-size       306 tracked modules within the 4000-token cap or their frozen baseline
comment-density   299 tracked modules within the 50% cap or their frozen share
noqa-debt         80 suppressions across 13 codes, each at its frozen count
vulture · wired-or-deleted · lint-imports · pyright (306 files, 0 errors)   all PASS
```

Every one of those is a **per-file or per-symbol** predicate. A tree can add fifty compliant modules and no gate notices, which is exactly what happened: the `factory-loop.md` section 9 baseline of "43 modules in a six-tier DAG" is now **86 modules**, and `basicly-tcmy`'s architectural findings were written against the smaller tree.

## Why this is not just another ratchet

The existing ratchets stop a file getting worse. They actively **reward** the growth this bead is about: the cheapest way to satisfy a module-size ratchet is to add a new module, which has no frozen baseline and starts clean. So the instrument that bounds file size is the instrument that drives module count, and nothing sits above the pair.

Note the interaction already paid for: extracting code out of an oversized module raises the remaining prose share and can trip comment-density, so an extraction only satisfies both gates when the extracted unit's prose share is above its origin's. A third signal on top of two that already fight each other must be designed with that in view, not bolted on.

## What it should measure

Deliberately open, because picking the metric before looking is how the six existing ratchets got their thresholds. Candidates, to be decided against this repo's own history rather than by preference:

- module count in `src/basicly/`
- total tracked tokens across all `.py`
- the ratio of the two, which is the one that discriminates *growth* from *redistribution* - splitting one module into two moves the first and leaves the third flat

Whichever is chosen, the requirement is the same: it must **not** be maskable by an action the per-file gates reward.

## What it must not be

Not a hard cap. The repo's own standing constraint is that a sizing control with no recorded correct firing becomes observability, and this signal has no firing history at all - it does not exist yet. So it ships **reporting and falsifiable**, recorded on the run and surfaced in the pass line, and earns the right to block only after it has refused something correctly. A prediction that blocks must be right; a prediction that reports costs nothing when it is wrong.

## Acceptance

- Given the current tree, when the signal is computed, then it reports a value and the window it was computed over, and does not fail any gate.
- Given a week in which N compliant new modules are added and no existing module grows, when the signal is computed, then it moves - so growth by addition is visible where the per-file ratchets are silent.
- Given a change that splits one module into two without adding code, when the signal is computed, then it distinguishes that from real growth rather than reporting them alike.
- Given the signal, when a supervised pass runs, then its value is recorded on the run and printed in the pass line, so it is falsifiable against the ledger.
- Given the signal has never refused anything, when it is evaluated, then it does not block - it is observability until it earns a firing.

## Scope

- `.scripts/`
- `basicly.toml`
- `tests/`

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly verify --mode fast` prints the tree signal and its window beside the existing per-file ratchet lines, and a seeded tree with added-but-compliant modules moves it.
payload.title: nothing bounds the tree so measure growth the per file ratchets cannot see

payload.description:
tests/test_rubrics.py::test_evaluate_deterministic_maps_exit_code fails on windows-latest CI. evaluate_deterministic splits the check command with shlex.split (posix), and the test embeds sys.executable, which on Windows is a backslash path (<redacted:windows-drive-path>). POSIX shlex treats backslash as an escape and mangles the path, so python is not found, the check exits non-zero, and the YES assertion fails. It is deterministic on Windows, not flaky.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Run pytest on Windows: tests/test_rubrics.py::test_evaluate_deterministic_maps_exit_code.
- The ok command {sys.executable} -c pass shlex-splits to a mangled path and exits non-zero.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The test builds the python path with forward slashes (Path(sys.executable).as_posix()) so posix shlex.split does not mangle it and Windows still accepts the executable path; both the YES and NO assertions hold on Windows and POSIX.
- No production change: realistic authored rubric commands use bare executables or forward-slash paths; a comment records why the test uses as_posix.
- pytest stays green on all platforms.
payload.title: Windows: deterministic rubric check test mangles the executable path via posix shlex

payload.description:
## Context

**The merge queue can destroy committed work and report success.** Measured twice on
2026-08-08, on two different lanes, in one session.

A lane that hits a conflict mid-build resolves it the obvious way — `git merge main` —
which produces a **merge commit whose resolution content exists in neither parent**.
The merge queue then lands the lane with `git rebase`, and `git rebase` **skips merge
commits by default** (`--rebase-merges` is not passed). The resolution evaporates. The
rebase prints `Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/<branch>` and exits 0.

## The two incidents

```text
basicly-u2hl.20   lost  src/basicly/handoff.py           demonstration field (D18)
                        .basicly/core/schemas/implementation-plan.schema.json
                        tests/test_handoff.py            incl. the control assertion
basicly-u2hl.14   lost  tests/test_artifact_record.py    the file its own gate needs
                        changelog.d/basicly-u2hl.14.added.md
```

## Why the test suite is not a backstop

**On `u2hl.20` the suite stayed green after the loss.** The feature and the tests that
covered it were in the same dropped merge commit, so removing both left a consistent,
passing tree that silently no longer did the thing the bead shipped. A gate cannot catch
this: there is nothing left to fail.

It was found only by pinning the pre-rebase tip and diffing:

```text
$ OLD=$(git rev-parse HEAD)          # before the rebase
$ git rebase main                    # "Successfully rebased"
$ comm -23 <(git ls-tree -r --name-only $OLD | sort) \
           <(git ls-tree -r --name-only HEAD | sort)
changelog.d/basicly-u2hl.14.added.md
tests/test_artifact_record.py
```

`u2hl.14`'s loss was load-bearing: the gate that bead ships is "one test file per source
module", and the dropped file was the test for a module main already carried, so the
lane would have shipped a gate its own tree fails.

## Steps to Reproduce

```text
1. Provision a lane worktree; commit work on the harness branch.
2. In the lane, `git merge main` and resolve a conflict by writing content that is in
   neither parent (any real conflict resolution).
3. `git rebase main` (what merge.py does at landing).
4. Observe: "Successfully rebased", exit 0, and the resolution is gone.
```

Expected: a landing either preserves the resolution or refuses, naming what it could
not carry. Never both drops it and reports success.

## Shape

Three candidates, and the choice is the design question:

1. **Detect and refuse.** Cheapest and safest: before rebasing, if the branch contains a
   merge commit, either bounce it back to the lane naming the merge, or take the
   diff-vs-first-parent route deliberately. Refusing is strictly better than silently
   dropping.
2. **`git rebase --rebase-merges`.** Preserves topology, but replays merges and can
   re-raise the same conflicts; needs its own conflict handling.
3. **Land by merge rather than rebase for branches that contain merges**, keeping rebase
   for the linear case.

Whichever is chosen, the **post-landing tree diff against the pre-rebase tip must become
a check**, because that is the only thing that actually caught this. A landing that drops
a tracked path present before the rebase and absent after, which main did not delete, is
a defect by construction.

Related but not the same: `basicly-3w51` (generated block bounces) is about *conflicts
recurring*; this is about a *resolution disappearing*.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane branch containing a merge commit whose resolution is in neither parent,
  when the merge queue lands it, then the resolution is present in the merged tree or
  the landing refuses naming the merge commit - check: a test builds exactly that branch
  shape, lands it, and asserts the resolution content is in the tree.
- Given any landing, when it completes, then no tracked path present before the rebase
  is absent after unless main deleted it - check: a test plants a file only in a merge
  commit and asserts the landing fails rather than silently dropping it.
- Given the failure mode, when it is reproduced, then the suite catches it without
  relying on the dropped code having surviving tests - check: the assertion is over the
  tree, not over behaviour.

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_merge.py -k rebase_merge_commit` fails on the current
implementation and passes after the fix; a real landing of a merge-carrying branch
either preserves the resolution or prints a refusal naming the commit.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `110000`
- depends on: none
payload.title: Stop the merge queue rebase from silently discarding a lane conflict resolution

payload.text:
Fixed 2026-08-09. Shape 1 (detect and refuse) plus the mandated post-replay tree check.

## What shipped

New module src/basicly/rebase.py owns getting a branch onto base. Two guards:

- merge_commits() refuses BEFORE the rebase runs, so nothing is destroyed and the message
  names the commit. --rebase-merges was rejected: it replays the merge and can re-raise the
  same conflicts with no attended resolver, and landing by merge would put an unreviewed
  second parent onto base. Handing it back to the lane loses nothing.
- dropped_paths() is the general backstop over the result, because refusing a known cause
  only covers the cause that is known. It subtracts paths base itself deleted (present at the
  merge base, absent in base) or every landing onto a base that deleted a file would report a
  false drop. On a drop the branch is reset to its pre-replay tip - a restoration, not a
  discard, since the target is the exact commit the replay started from.

Statuses rebase-merge-commit and rebase-dropped-paths are in PRE_GATE_STATUSES (so a one-shot
gate override survives) and deliberately NOT in CONFLICT_STATUSES: a branch git would mangle
is a branch-shape defect, not a missed scope coupling, and routing it there would record a
 edge against a lane that collided with nobody.

## The extraction this forced, which was not optional

src/basicly/merge.py was frozen at 15,401 tokens and tests/test_merge.py at 19,737, so neither
could grow by a line. The seam taken is cohesive and related, not an unrelated refactor:
'getting the branch onto base' against 'merging it into base'. rebuild_generated_conflicts and
unmerged_paths moved with it (both were private to merge.py, no external callers), and
rebase.py does not import back - merge.py maps ReplayOutcome onto its own MergeResult.

Knock-ons all real, none optional: .importlinter is exhaustive so the new module needed a tier
(placed below merge, above config|worktree); the docs-claims generated block moved 79 -> 80
engine modules; the test-naming gate required tests/test_rebase.py.

## Deviation from this bead's stated demonstration

The bead names `pytest tests/test_merge.py -k rebase_merge_commit`. The tests are in
tests/test_rebase.py instead, because the test-naming gate refuses tests for a new module left
in the file named after the module it was extracted from. Five generated-conflict tests moved
there too and were rewritten against rebase.replay directly rather than through
merge_worktree, which is the layer that now owns the behaviour.

## Evidence

Tests are against a REAL git repo, deliberately: a stubbed git cannot skip a merge commit, so
a fake could only assert we called rev-list --merges, never that the thing being guarded
against happens.

- Positive control test_a_plain_rebase_really_does_discard_the_resolution reproduces the loss
  with the old path and asserts git exits 0 while doing it. If git ever stops skipping merge
  commits this fails and the guards become dead weight - the only way anyone would find out.
- test_replay_restores_the_branch_when_the_backstop_fires blinds guard 1 by injection to prove
  guard 2 independently catches and undoes the loss.
- test_dropped_paths_ignores_a_file_base_deleted is the discriminator for the subtraction; a
  guard that cries wolf gets switched off.
- The fixture had to be corrected mid-work: a lane whose OWN commits conflict does not
  reproduce this, it just bounces. The loss is silent precisely because the lane's commits
  replay cleanly and only the merge carries content, so the fixture uses git merge --no-commit.

Gates: basicly verify --mode full = 21/21 PASS. pytest 3611 passed (+7: 12 new, 5 relocated).

Exercised as a consumer, not only as a test - a real repo, a real git worktree, a real
merge-carrying branch, landed through merge.merge_worktree:

  status : rebase-merge-commit
  detail : harness/feat carries 1 merge commit(s) `git rebase` would skip, discarding any
           resolution held only there: c523ab05... Linearize the branch and re-land.
  branch unmoved: True   resolution intact: 'resolved: neither s

Correction to the comment above: line 22 reads " edge against a lane that collided with
nobody" because a backtick pair was eaten by the shell. It should read "a `related` edge
against a lane that collided with nobody" - COUPLING_DEP_TYPE, the non-gating dependency the
queue records for a missed coupling.

payload.description:
Retro finding from the 2026-07-18 foundry-followon session (basicly-58iu). While investigating br behavior (what `br lint` flags, a `br show --json` key name), throwaway beads were created and `br delete`d. `br delete` leaves a TOMBSTONE row in `.beads/issues.jsonl`, which the harness loop's tracker-state commit then captures — so junk probe beads reach the project tracker history unless pruned. `--ephemeral` is not a workaround: ephemeral beads do not export to JSONL but `br lint` also will not lint them (`total:0`), so a lint probe needs a real bead.

Put this guidance where the next agent authoring br probes will see it: add a short note to the `tool-br` skill (or a quirks fragment) covering the trap and the avoidance. There is no `br compact`/`purge`/`gc`; the only clean prune is `br delete <id> --hard --force` ("prunes tombstones from JSONL immediately").

## Acceptance Criteria

- The `tool-br` skill (or a quirks fragment) gains a concise note: investigating br by creating+deleting real beads leaves tombstones the loop commits; prune with `br delete --hard`, or avoid probing the live tracker; ephemeral beads are not linted.
- Authored as YAML catalog source and projected (`basicly skills-build`/`build`); `basicly catalog lint` and the relevant `*-check` gate pass.
- Fits within the always-on budget if placed in an applies_to:[all] fragment (prefer the on-demand tool-br skill to avoid baseline growth).

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a projected agent instruction surface when an agent chooses a model tier for dispatched work then the guidance states the four-tier ladder with its per-provider classes and the rule that cost is measured per landed correct change so a tier is chosen for reliability rather than sticker price with the projection gates green and the always-on budget not regressed
payload.description:
## Context

Session retro 2026-07-25, from the owner correcting `docs/agent-roster-design.md`. The design shipped a three-way cheap/mid/high tier split and the rule "route to the cheapest sufficient model", plus a persona justified as "cheap tokens replacing expensive ones". Two things were wrong and the owner corrected both:

1. Providers ship three-to-four capability classes with concrete names (claude: haiku, sonnet, opus, fable - opus the workhorse, fable the designer/architect; GPT: luna, terra, sol), so a three-way generic split does not map onto anything real.
2. A cheaper model is not cheaper work. Its mistakes come back as rework dispatches, extra review cycles, bounced merges and human attention, all charged to the same change - so the cheap dispatch routinely produces the expensive outcome. The unit of cost is total tokens plus wall-clock plus human interventions per landed correct change, never the price of one dispatch.

Root cause worth fixing in prose, not just in that document: nothing the harness distributes states the unit of cost or the tier ladder, so every agent that picks a model - and the roster design itself - reasons from per-dispatch sticker price. The correction is already argued in `docs/agent-roster-design.md` section R5 (basicly-eqp6); this bead is about distributing it as catalog guidance for the agents that act on it.

Constraint to respect: the always-on baseline is at its soft cap (see basicly-c5to), so this must be a scoped fragment or a skill section, not another `applies_to: [all]` fragment - or it has to pay for itself by trimming something.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a projected agent instruction surface when an agent chooses a model tier for dispatched work then the guidance states the four-tier ladder with its per-provider classes and the rule that cost is measured per landed correct change so a tier is chosen for reliability rather than sticker price with the projection gates green and the always-on budget not regressed

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/fragments/**`

payload.description:
## Trigger

When the definition-of-ready gate asks a record for its requirements, I want it to ask only records created after the rule existed, so I can stop refusing 341 records for content nobody could have written.

Measured 2026-09-18 over the folded ledger: all 341 open records owe requirements, 0 carry the field and 0 carry a heading to migrate from. The engine seam could not write that field until basicly-77tjvmk, so the debt was never a lapse, it was impossible. Retro-filling 341 statements would be inventing content, which is the guess you keep.

The discriminator may not be a timestamp. Section 9.5 forbids deriving anything from the clock, and there is no global ordering across records because sequence numbers are per item. So the rule binds on a marker the producer writes at create: a record minted under the rule carries it, an older one does not, and absence is unambiguous because every new record gets it.

The debt stays visible rather than being forgiven. owed still reports requirements for an unmarked record, so the board keeps showing it; only the refusal is withheld.
payload.requirements: the marker is a field the producer writes, never a clock reading and never a global sequence, because neither exists per record. No engine import, standard library only, Python 3.9 floor. No record already in the ledger is rewritten: the rule reads what is there.
payload.title: require requirements only of records minted under the rule

payload.description:
## Trigger

When the engine lands a unit of work, I want it to fold every pending writer shard into the trunk log in the same commit, so I can stop running compact by hand and the specification stops claiming something the code does not do.

SPEC.md section 4.0 states 'The engine's landing calls the same function; it is a caller, not a second mechanism'. That is false as shipped in basicly-v5zvsh1. A grep for compact across src/basicly finds only an unrelated number formatter in board_footer.py. The claim was written into the specification in the same commit that failed to wire it, and docs-claims passed because it catches an invented command and not a claim about a call that does not exist. Compaction was run by hand three times during that session without the gap being noticed.

Scope note, recorded so a later reader does not overclaim. In the engine model the base checkout on main is the only committer of tracker state and a lane's worktree redirects its ledger to that same directory, so sharding buys the engine tidiness rather than merge safety. The merge safety it buys is for the standalone consumer who commits the ledger on a feature branch. Both are true and they are not the same claim.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The engine's tracker-state commit folds every pending shard into the trunk log and stages the removal and the append in one commit.
- A tree holding foreign dirt is left alone, exactly as the existing refusal already does, so compaction never runs in a tree the loop does not own.
- The SPEC section 4.0 sentence is true against the code, or it is rewritten to state what is true.
- A test asserts the landing leaves no pending shard behind, against a positive control that shows one present before it.
payload.title: fold pending shards at the engine landing so the spec claim is true

payload.text: Wired at tracker._commit_tracker_state through the tracker seam rather than from merge.py directly. The first attempt reached owned_store.kit from merge.py and test_gate_source refused it: the store is reachable only from its own seam modules, and merge.py is not one. The gate was right and the functions moved to tracker.py, which merge.py already calls for scrub_ledger.

payload.name: close_reason
payload.value: shipped: the landing folds every shard, the spec line is true against the code, and the foreign-dirt refusal is asserted to leave a shard alone

## Context

- `.basicly/core/kit/board/**`

- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`
- `changelog.d/<this-id>.added.md`

## Context

Owner directive 2026-08-28: the board must become a cockpit for developers as well as an observability surface for operations. basicly-k6tpep answers the operator question "what is happening right now, and does it need me?". A developer asks a different question: "where is my record, what is being done to it, and what stands between it and main?" This record is the inspect half of basicly-lc2bd3v, the cockpit epic, and it answers operator question 5 of nine, "what one record actually says". `tests/test_board_operator_questions.py` xfails that question against this id, so closing this record without moving the question is itself a failure.

## The data path, decided 2026-09-06

The detail renders **from the snapshot**, not from a per-request subprocess. basicly-lc2bd3v argued for the `board_actions.ACTIONS` seam on the ground that "294 bodies would be a snapshot nobody can serve" - that argument is about record **bodies**, and the fields below are metadata. Measured 2026-09-06: `units[]` carries 7 fields for 295 records and the whole snapshot is 172 KB.

The snapshot path is what the demonstration requires: `basicly board --out` writes a self-contained file with no server behind it, so a page that shells out cannot be demonstrated that way.

The `consumer-reads-only-the-snapshot` contract is unaffected either way: it binds `board_actions`, `board_asks`, `board_diagram`, `board_footer`, `board_graph`, `board_loop`, `board_regions`, `board_render` and `board_wall`. `board_serve`, `board_facts` and `board_snapshot` are producers and are not in its source list.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a developer opens `<redacted:posix-absolute-path><id>` on the board, IT SHALL show the record's title, status, priority, derived phase, worktree and branch, the checkpoints held and missing, the rework count per gate, the open blockers and the open dependents, from one snapshot read.

The page itself goes in a new module rather than into `board_regions.py` (754 lines) or `board_facts.py` (660), both of which carry frozen `module-size` entries and have open split records against them (`basicly-k6tpep.1`, `basicly-k6tpep.2`).

## Context

Owner directive 2026-08-28: the board must become a cockpit for developers as well as an observability surface for operations. basicly-k6tpep answers the operator question "what is happening right now, and does it need me?". A developer asks a different question: "where is my record, what is being done to it, and what stands between it and main?" Today that answer needs `basicly loop status`, `basicly tracker show` and the worktree list, read separately.

This record is the inspect half of basicly-lc2bd3v, the cockpit epic, and it answers operator question 5 of nine, "what one record actually says". `tests/test_board_operator_questions.py` xfails that question against this id, so closing this record without moving the question is itself a failure.

## The data path, decided 2026-09-06

The detail renders **from the snapshot**, not from a per-request subprocess. basicly-lc2bd3v argued for the `board_actions.ACTIONS` seam on the ground that "294 bodies would be a snapshot nobody can serve" - that argument is about record **bodies**, and the fields below are metadata. Measured 2026-09-06: `units[]` carries 7 fields for 295 records and the whole snapshot is 172 KB.

The snapshot path is what the demonstration requires: `basicly board --out` writes a self-contained file with no server behind it, so a page that shells out cannot be demonstrated that way.

The `consumer-reads-only-the-snapshot` contract is unaffected either way: it binds `board_actions`, `board_asks`, `board_diagram`, `board_footer`, `board_graph`, `board_loop`, `board_regions`, `board_render` and `board_wall`. `board_serve`, `board_facts` and `board_snapshot` are producers and are not in its source list.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a developer opens `<redacted:posix-absolute-path><id>` on the board, IT SHALL show the record's title, status, priority, derived phase, worktree and branch, the checkpoints held and missing, the rework count per gate, the open blockers and the open dependents, from one snapshot read.
- WHEN a lane is running for that record, the same page SHALL show the agent, the model, the start time, the last progress line and the spend so far, and SHALL say when the snapshot was taken.
- WHEN the record has no lane, the page SHALL say so and SHALL name the next command that moves it, copied from the engine's own remedy text and never composed by the board.
- WHEN the snapshot lacks a field the page needs, the field SHALL render as absent, never as a default value, and the `harness-board/v1` contract SHALL name the added sections.
- WHERE the board prints a record id - next up, running now, parked, claimed, events, asks - THAT ID SHALL be the link to that record's page, so the page has a way in from the wall.
- WHERE a row clips a record title to fit its column, THE ROW SHALL carry the untruncated title as a `title` attribute, so a reader recovers it without leaving the board.

## Scope

Widened at the landing on 2026-09-06, after the scope gate named fourteen files. Every one is
this record's own work rather than drift: the producer is layered, and a `detail` section on
the contract plus a page that links every printed id reaches further than the first list
guessed. `board_advance.remedy` had to stop being private so the page could copy the engine's
remedy text instead of composing it; `board_cli._write_records` writes the pages the
demonstration opens; `board_footer.EventLine` splits the id out of a ticker line so the link
lands on the id and not on a substring; `board_sections.DetailFacts` is the contract section
itself; and a new board consumer must join `.importlinter` or the contract check is silently
not made about the one module this record adds.

The previous list also named `.basicly/core/kit/board/**`, which matched no file on disk.

## Working Set

What a lane must read to build this, priced by the band instead of `## Scope`. The two
differ on purpose. `## Scope` is every path the work writes, which the landing scope gate
holds it to. This is the smaller set the lane holds in its head, and the band's own
constant says a corrected declaration is answered by declaring the working set rather than
by raising the ceiling.

Out of it: `docs/architecture/architecture.md`, to which this lane appends one status row
and which it does not read to build a page; and the two per-lane fragments, which are
written from a template and read by nothing.

payload.description:
## Context

Agent hooks are projected per family by `hooks.yaml`'s `manager` field, and the two
families are **not** at parity [M 2026-08-08]:

```text
manager: claude    protect-generated      stage=pretooluse
manager: claude    tool-usage             stage=posttooluse
manager: copilot   tool-usage-copilot     stage=posttooluse
```

So a consumer on Copilot gets the telemetry hook and **not the guard**.
`protect-generated` refuses an edit to a generated file at tool time; on Copilot that
edit is caught only later, by the `protect-generated-commit` git hook. The git floor
still holds, so nothing is unsafe — but the earlier refusal, which is the whole point
of an agent hook (`factory-loop.md` section 3.3: source inspection beats successive),
is Claude-only.

## The premise that blocked this, and why it is gone

The repo believed Copilot had **no hook surface at all**. That claim was recorded in the
tier kit and repeated into `architecture.md`, and it was **wrong** — an artifact of a
probe that looked for a `hooks/` directory under `~/.copilot`, a hook key in a
`settings.json` that simply had none set, and a `--help` that does not enumerate config
keys. None of the three was a positive control.

Corrected and fetched from the vendor 2026-08-08:

```text
config          .github/hooks/*.json  |  settings.json "hooks"  |  config.json "hooks"
                config.json "disableAllHooks" turns them all off
events          sessionStart  sessionEnd  userPromptSubmitted
                preToolUse  postToolUse  errorOccurred
preToolUse      documented as able to APPROVE or DENY a tool call
```

`preToolUse` approving or denying is exactly what `protect-generated` needs, so this is
extension rather than invention — the projection layer already routes by `manager` and
already writes a managed `.github/hooks/basicly-<id>.json`.

## What this bead is NOT

**It does not resolve tier injection.** That needs a hook to *modify* a spawn's
arguments, not to approve or deny one, and no copilot hook has been shown to fire for an
agent spawn at all (three probes on 1.0.77, `basicly-wbsz`). Approve/deny and modify are
different capabilities; keep them apart. The tier kit's static fallback stands until
someone demonstrates a spawn-time rewrite.

## Constraints

- **The git hooks remain the deterministic floor.** An agent hook is an earlier surface,
  never a replacement — a consumer on a host without one must still get the same
  guarantee at commit time.
- **Parity is a claim on a consumer surface, so it must be exercised, not asserted.**
  `basicly-irrm` already caught this shape once when the README advertised three agents
  and the ledger held dispatches for one. A projected hook that never fires is the
  instrument-built-and-never-connected defect this repo keeps rediscovering.

payload.name: description
payload.value:
## Trigger

When a hook declared manager claude has a copilot equivalent stage but Copilot only receives the telemetry hook, I want protect-generated projected to Copilot too, so I can gate the two agent families alike before the git floor has to catch it later.

## Context

Agent hooks are projected per family by `hooks.yaml`'s `manager` field, and the two
families are **not** at parity [M 2026-08-08]:

```text
manager: claude    protect-generated      stage=pretooluse
manager: claude    tool-usage             stage=posttooluse
manager: copilot   tool-usage-copilot     stage=posttooluse
```

So a consumer on Copilot gets the telemetry hook and **not the guard**.
`protect-generated` refuses an edit to a generated file at tool time; on Copilot that
edit is caught only later, by the `protect-generated-commit` git hook. The git floor
still holds, so nothing is unsafe — but the earlier refusal, which is the whole point
of an agent hook (`factory-loop.md` section 3.3: source inspection beats successive),
is Claude-only.

## The premise that blocked this, and why it is gone

The repo believed Copilot had **no hook surface at all**. That claim was recorded in the
tier kit and repeated into `architecture.md`, and it was **wrong** — an artifact of a
probe that looked for a `hooks/` directory under `~/.copilot`, a hook key in a
`settings.json` that simply had none set, and a `--help` that does not enumerate config
keys. None of the three was a positive control.

Corrected and fetched from the vendor 2026-08-08:

```text
config          .github/hooks/*.json  |  settings.json "hooks"  |  config.json "hooks"
                config.json "disableAllHooks" turns them all off
events          sessionStart  sessionEnd  userPromptSubmitted
                preToolUse  postToolUse  errorOccurred
preToolUse      documented as able to APPROVE or DENY a tool call
```

`preToolUse` approving or denying is exactly what `protect-generated` needs, so this is
extension rather than invention — the projection layer already routes by `manager` and
already writes a managed `.github/hooks/basicly-<id>.json`.

## What this bead is NOT

**It does not resolve tier injection.** That needs a hook to *modify* a spawn's
arguments, not to approve or deny one, and no copilot hook has been shown to fire for an
agent spawn at all (three probes on 1.0.77, `basicly-wbsz`). Approve/deny and modify are
different capabilities; keep them apart. The tier kit's static fallback stands until
someone demonstrates a spawn-time rewrite.

## Constraints

- **The git hooks remain the deterministic floor.** An agent hook is an earlier surface,
  never a replacement — a consumer on a host without one must still get the same
  guarantee at commit time.
- **Parity is a claim on a consumer surface, so it must be exercised, not asserted.**
  `basicly-irrm` already caught this shape once when the README advertised three agents
  and the ledger held dispatches for one. A projected hook that never fires is the
  instrument-built-and-never-connected defect this repo keeps rediscovering.
- Event names are the vendor's and change without our involvement; treat the mapping
  from `stage` to a copilot event as data, re-probed rather than recalled.

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly hooks-build && uv run basicly hooks-check` writes and verifies a copilot
`preToolUse` guard, and `ls .github/hooks/` shows it beside the existing telemetry hook.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/hooks/hooks.yaml`
- `src/basicly/hooks.py`
- `tests/test_hooks.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `90000`
- depends on: none

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given a hook declared `manager: claude` with a stage that has a copilot equivalent,
  when the projection runs, then an equivalent copilot hook is written - check: a test
  asserts `protect-generated` produces a `.github/hooks/` entry on `preToolUse`.
- Given the projected copilot guard, when an agent edits a generated file, then the edit
  is refused before it lands - check: drive the hook with a real `preToolUse` payload
  naming a generated path and assert the deny response; and exercise it in a live
  session, since a projected hook that never fires is the defect this bead exists to
  avoid.
- Given a stage with no copilot equivalent, when the projection runs, then it declines
  and says why rather than writing a hook that cannot fire - check: a test asserts the
  decline path and its message.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane branch whose diff adds a config schema entry and declares that key in the repos own config when the landing runs then it either lands or fails with a message naming the schema before declaration ordering rule and a regression test proves the bare unknown key refusal red first
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

Measured 2026-08-06 landing `basicly-o8p0`, whose single commit added a
`[worktree] append_only_paths` key to `config.CONFIG_SCHEMA` **and** declared it in
this repo's `basicly.toml`:

```
uv run basicly loop run basicly-o8p0 --root basicly-yc0x --autonomy L3
Error: basicly.toml: unknown key 'append_only_paths' in [worktree];
       [worktree] accepts base_branch, concurrency
basicly 0.6.0 refuses a config name it cannot honour rather than ignoring it ...
```

Observed — the landing died before verify ran. State at that moment:

| Where | `basicly.toml` has the key | `config.py` knows the key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| base checkout | no | no |
| lane worktree | **yes** | **yes** |

Expected — a lane that adds a config key and uses it can land.

## Cause: the landing runs the base engine against the worktree's config

`loop run` is invoked from the base checkout, so `uv run basicly` resolves the entry
point to **base's** `src/basicly/`, and that process then reads the **worktree's**
`basicly.toml` when it verifies the rebased tree. Base's schema has no
`append_only_paths`, and `basicly-1piy` — which landed hours earlier the same day —
made an unknown key a hard refusal rather than a silent ignore. So the pre-merge
engine validates the post-merge config and refuses it.

This is the same mechanism the `harness-loop` runbook already records — "`loop run`
imports `merge`/`verify`/`loop` from base at process start and never reloads them", so
a change to landing-scoring code is scored by the pre-merge version — but it is
**fatal rather than merely misleading**, and it reaches `config`, which every command
loads.

## Scope of the block

Any bead whose diff adds a `CONFIG_SCHEMA` entry and declares it in `basicly.toml`
cannot land in one commit. That is a standing tax on config-carrying work, and this
release ladder has several such beads ahead of it — `o486` (band calibration),
`3ifz` (learned parameters), and the roster's `[runner.roles]` section all add keys.

`basicly-1piy` is not wrong. Its commit message records that staged
warn-then-error was considered and rejected for consumers, with reasons that hold:
an engine that cannot honour a key and runs anyway is the defect it fixed. What the
note did not consider is **our own lanes**, where the reader and the file are one
commit apart by construction.

## Fix shape, cheapest first

- **Document the ordering rule and let it stand**: schema lands first, the
  declaration follows in a second landing. That is what unblocked `o8p0`, it costs one
  extra landing, and it needs no code. It belongs in the `harness-loop` skill beside
  the existing pre-merge-code warning, because nothing currently tells a lane author.
- **Or make the landing's config read tolerant of a key the merged tree introduces**:
  validate the worktree's config with the *worktree's* schema, since that is the code
  about to become base. This is the correct fix and the larger one — the landing would
  have to resolve the schema from the tree under test rather than from the running
  process.

Deliberately **not** proposed: relaxing `1piy`'s refusal to a warning. That reinstates
the defect it fixed, where the file states one behaviour and the engine performs
another.

## Regression test

Proven red first (`basicly-kjc5.49`): a lane branch whose diff adds a schema entry and
declares it must either land, or fail with a message that names the ordering rule —
not with a bare unknown-key refusal that reads as a config typo.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/verify.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`
- `.basicly/core/skills/harness-loop/skill.yaml`
payload.title: A lane that adds a config key and declares it cannot land in one commit

payload.text:
Reproduced a second time on 2026-08-06, landing basicly-lpsf:

routed: basicly-lpsf -> error - routing failed: basicly.toml: unknown key
'quiet_after' in [runner]; [runner] accepts agents, context_windows,
copilot_session_store, decider, default, default_tier, max_agent_processes,
runner_timeout, stall_after

Same shape as the basicly-o8p0 occurrence: the lane's single commit added quiet_after to
CONFIG_SCHEMA and declared it in basicly.toml, and the landing died before verify ran.
Two things this occurrence adds.

It cost more than one extra landing this time. The lane had already hit runner_timeout at
1800s having spent 25595734 tokens, so commit.salvage committed the worktree and the
refusal landed on top of a run that was already terminal. The failure was therefore
invisible until after the full spend, and the reported cause named a config key rather
than the ordering rule - which reads as a config typo, exactly as this bead predicts.

The workaround held and cost nothing, but by luck rather than design. The declaration was
deferred to a second landing and that was free because DEFAULT_QUIET_AFTER is already
1800.0, so the merged engine used the same value the declaration would have set. A key
whose declared value differed from its default would have landed with the wrong behaviour
for one landing, silently. Worth stating in the fix: the documented ordering rule is only
behaviour-neutral when the deferred declaration equals the schema default, and nothing
checks that.

Reproduced a THIRD time, 2026-08-07, on basicly-vkh0.19's landing. The lane added [tracker] mode = 'external' to basicly.toml in the same commit that taught CONFIG_SCHEMA the section, and loop advance refused it:

  Error: basicly.toml: unknown section 'tracker'; this file's sections are [catalog], [paths], [policy], [privacy], [runner], [verify], [worktree]

Mechanism confirmed: loop advance imports the engine from base at process start, so the version validating the config is the pre-merge one, and it refuses an unknown name by design. Same root as basicly-kjc5.57 (a change to the landing logic cannot take effect on the landing that merges it) - this is that shape applied to the config schema rather than to the landing code.

Workaround used, and its safety condition CHECKED rather than assumed this time: the declaration was deferred to a second commit on base (4e592a7) after the schema landed at 60ddf4d. The bead notes the workaround is only behaviour-neutral when the deferred value equals the schema default and that nothing checks it. Here it does - the declared value is 'external' and br.DEFAULT_TRACKER_MODE is MODE_EXTERNAL, confirmed by calling config.load_tracker_mode with the block present and absent and getting the same answer.

So the workaround held, but only because a human verified the equality the bead says is unchecked. A lane declaring a NON-default value cannot use it, and would need either a two-release deprecation or a schema that tolerates a forward-unknown section for one version. That is the choice this bead still has to make.

Reproduced a FOURTH time 2026-08-07, landing basicly-m4zv.2 on a three-lane supervised pass of basicly-m4zv. This is the first occurrence where the documented workaround does not apply, so the bead's 'cheapest first' fix shape is now insufficient on its own.

routed: basicly-m4zv.2 -> error - routing failed: basicly.toml: unknown key 'rank1_floor' in [catalog]; [catalog] accepts technologies

Same mechanism as basicly-o8p0 and basicly-lpsf: the single commit adds rank1_floor and rank1_floor_high_water to CONFIG_SCHEMA and declares both in basicly.toml, and the landing validates the worktree config with the pre-merge base engine.

WHAT IS NEW. The recorded workaround - schema lands first, declaration follows in a second landing - CANNOT be applied here, and this is the non-default-value case the previous note predicted had no route. Four repo-state tests require the declaration to be present, so a schema-only landing fails verify instead:

  tests/test_catalog_lint.py::test_the_shipped_catalog_clears_its_own_declared_floor
  tests/test_catalog_lint.py::test_the_declared_floor_leaves_headroom_below_the_measured_rate
  tests/test_cli.py::test_cli_catalog_verify_passes
  tests/test_cli.py::test_cli_build_verify_passes_on_clean_catalog

Both orderings therefore fail: declaration-in-lane dies before verify on the unknown key, schema-first dies at verify on those four tests. Measured directly - appending the two keys to base's basicly.toml and running 'uv run basicly check' from base reproduces the refusal in one command, and the lane worktree with schema and declaration together is green at 3103 passed.

COST. One re-dispatch of the lane (3 run records, 16,465,591 tokens total against a 14,036,709 first pass) plus a hand landing: rebase onto main, verify green in the worktree, git merge --no-ff from base, then 'basicly verify --mode full --issue' from base with the merged engine, which passed every gate and recorded verify=pass. Shipped normally after that.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX SHAPE. Documenting the ordering rule is no longer sufficient as the cheap option, because a bead whose tests assert the declared value has no ordering that works. The second option in this bead - validate the worktree's config with the worktree's schema, since that is the code about to become base - is now the only fix that covers this class.

payload.description:
## Context

Observed 2026-08-23: a git push from base ran the pre-push hook while a live supervisor held unstaged ledger dirt. The hook printed 'Unstaged files detected' and stashed .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl to a pre-commit cache patch; the push was killed at a 2-minute timeout mid-hook, and the stash was never restored. One engine event (the basicly-mdv1qu worktree binding, external_ref seq 7) vanished from the working tree while the lane it bound was running. Recovered by git-applying the cache patch by hand; loop status confirmed the binding after. The window is structural: the ledger is append-only shared state that a second process writes between stash and restore, so even an uninterrupted hook can restore the patch over newer appends.

## Steps to Reproduce

Start a supervise pass (it leaves ledger events unstaged in base), run git push from base, interrupt the pre-push hook after the stash line.

## Acceptance Criteria

Given the pre-push hook runs with unstaged changes confined to .basicly/ledger/ then it does not stash them and runs against the tree as it stands.
Given unstaged changes outside the ledger then the stash behaviour is unchanged.
Given a hook interruption after a stash then the ledger file is byte-identical to before the hook started.
Demonstrated by: a test that dirties only the ledger, runs the pre-push script, kills it mid-run, and asserts the ledger file is unchanged.

## Scope

- `.pre-commit-config.yaml`
- `.scripts/`

payload.description:
## Context

Owner requirement 2026-08-22: *"there is no actual diagramatic visualization of the loop with artifacts and important information about the factory loop and workflow."*

Today the region is seven boxes with counts. Designed by a Fable 5 architect against the engine rather than against the architecture prose.

## The authority check came out clean

`loop_state.py:31` lists `intake, classify, decompose, build, verify, validate, ship, done`, and `architecture.md:1417-1440` states the same eight with `done` terminal and repair and retrospective explicitly **not** phases. They agree, so there is no vocabulary finding to fix first. Phase is never stored: it is derived per read from five tracker facts (`loop_state.py:140-191`).

Three human checkpoints exist - classify, decompose, ship (`config.py:391`). Gates are engine verdicts, checkpoints are human approvals. **`build -> verify` is the only merge in the whole loop** (`loop.py:1481-1550`).

## Mermaid is refused, decisively

`tests/test_board_render.py:95-107` asserts `"<script" not in page`. Mermaid is a JavaScript runtime renderer, so even vendored inline it is refused by a gate that already exists. The repo's own `.scripts/render_mermaid.mjs` states in its header that jsdom's shimmed measurements mean *the geometry of the output means nothing* - it is a **validity** gate, not a layout engine. Mermaid stays docs-only.

## Inline SVG is the answer, and it fixes the tofu permanently

Assembled as strings by the render layer exactly like the existing HTML. No script, no link, no src, so it passes the no-external-origin gate by construction. Markers become drawn shapes rather than codepoints, so **the glyph channel stops depending on font coverage** - which is the root of the owner's tofu complaint. `viewBox="0 0 1200 400"`, station geometry static, only tokens and badges and edge labels data-driven.

## What feeds it, field by field

| element | field | live value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| count per phase node | `units[].phase` | intake 220, classify 1, decompose 21, build 2, verify 1 |
| lane markers with agent and model | `lanes[].phase/agent/model` | two under BUILD |
| gate weather on the landing edge | `gates.checks[]` | 36 checks, 2 failing |
| waiting flag on a node | `asks[]` where `subject` equals a phase name | ship, 1 waiting, 6.9 days |
| feed and sink | `backlog.ready`, `repo.branch/head` | 189 ready, main |

**Two stated data gaps, not guesses.** No artifact field exists anywhere on the snapshot contract, so the diagram can *name* the artifact each edge produces and can never colour it approved or pending. And the ask-to-phase pin relies on `subject` happening to equal a phase name - true today, heuristic by contract; when it does not match, the ask appears in the alarm band only.

**The scoping fix the region needs.** `board_regions.py:209-238` counts every `units` row, which is why 220 sit at intake - intake is the derivation's `otherwise` rung (`loop_state.py:191`). Draw intake as the hopper feeding the diagram rather than as a station.

**Pass scope cannot come from the graph, and this was tested rather than assumed.** `session.root` has 102 parent-child descendants and **neither live lane is among them**, because the supervisor adopted them by label, outside the subtree. The honest pass scope on current data is `lanes[]` union `asks[]` union `units where phase != intake`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN the region renders, IT SHALL show the phases, the gate on each transition, the human checkpoints and the artifact each edge produces, as a diagram rather than a histogram.
- WHEN a unit is in flight, ITS POSITION SHALL be drawn, and a lane an agent is inside SHALL be distinguishable from a unit merely resting at that phase.
- WHEN a human is the blocker, THE NODE THEY BLOCK SHALL carry it with its age.
- WHEN the landing gate is red, THE MERGE EDGE SHALL say so, because that is the next thing that will fail.
- WHERE a fact is not on the snapshot contract, THE DIAGRAM SHALL NOT imply it, and the record SHALL name the producer change it would need.
- WHERE the region draws counts, INTAKE SHALL NOT be a station, because it is the derivation's default rung and its count is the untouched backlog.
- WHERE any mark is drawn, IT SHALL be a shape rather than a codepoint, and the page SHALL reference no external origin.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_regions.py`
- `src/basicly/board_render.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/board_page.html.j2`
- `tests/test_board_regions.py`
- `tests/test_board_render.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `140000`
- depends on: `basicly-ibzr0f`
- demonstration: Render the board with a supervised pass live and read the diagram against the supervisor's own reported lane set, the gate summary and the pending ask - then run the overflow instrument at 1280, 1600 and 1920 reading both signals, having fired it on its own fixtures first.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a subprocess whose output is not decodable in the hosts preferred encoding when the engine captures it then the bytes are decoded as utf-8 explicitly and the text arrives intact or the failure raises rather than returning success with no output and given a test for it then the assertion is a real subprocess round trip with the encoding injected as test data rather than a parsed string on a utf-8 host
payload.description:
## Decision, 2026-08-06: adopted as a present defect, NOT as a section 12 requirement

The handover proposed this as a design rule for the replacement tracker. **Narrowed on
review**, and the narrowing is the point:

- **Adopted** for the call sites that exist today. They are real, verified, and one of them
  biases a decision we are about to take.
- **Declined** as a section 12 requirement. Section 4 puts the replacement in-process and pure
  Python, so its own ledger reads use no subprocess at all. Writing a process-boundary rule for
  a component whose design removes the boundary is a requirement with no subject - the kind of
  speculative rule this repo's core rules forbid.

So this is a bug against the current adapter, not a change to the tracker design. If the
replacement ever shells out, section 12 gains the rule then, with a subject.

## The mechanism - established, not inferred

Reproduced on Windows with Python 3.14 where the preferred encoding is `cp1252`, against a
child writing a word whose UTF-8 encoding contains byte `0x81`:

| Configuration | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `capture_output=True, text=True` | returncode 0, `stdout` is `None`, **nothing raised** |
| `stdout=PIPE, text=True` | raises `UnicodeDecodeError` - loud |
| `capture_output=True` then `.decode("utf-8")` | the text, intact |

With **both** pipes captured, `communicate()` decodes on reader *threads*, so the
`UnicodeDecodeError` kills a thread instead of propagating. The caller sees success and no
output. Piping only stdout raises properly - **the safe-looking, more convenient call is the
silent one**, which is why this survives review.

## Call sites, verified in this repo 2026-08-06

- `src/basicly/br.py:106-107` - the single seam the engine reaches the tracker through, in
  exactly the silent configuration: `subprocess.run([br_path, *args], cwd=repo_root,
  capture_output=True, text=True, check=False)`. **Every `run_br` call inherits it.**
- `src/basicly/tracker_surface.py:112` and `:127` - same configuration, on the telemetry path
  section 6 gates the schema decision on. **This is the sharpest consequence**: telemetry that
  silently under-reports would bias the decision, and the bias is invisible because the failure
  mode is an empty read that looks like an empty result.
- Seven files under `src/basicly/` pass `text=True` to a subprocess.
- `src/basicly/fleet.py` has **no** subprocess - it reads run records as files. So a future
  peer read would *introduce* this boundary where fleet does not have it, and `br.py:107` is
  the pattern a new reader would most likely be copied from.

## Why it is worth fixing now rather than waiting for cutover

The `br` adapter exists only until the replacement lands, which argues for leaving it. Against
that: `tracker_surface` is not the adapter, it is the instrument measuring the surface the
replacement will be designed against, and section 6 makes that measurement an input to the
schema decision. An instrument that fails silent is worse than no instrument, because a zero
reads as a measurement.

## The assertion this needs

**A test asserting on parsed strings cannot see this**, and neither can a suite that only runs
on a UTF-8 host. The assertion must be a **real subprocess round trip** with a non-UTF-8
preferred encoding injected as test data - per this repo's platform-hermetic rule, by injection
rather than by racing a host.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/br.py`
- `src/basicly/tracker_surface.py`
- `tests/test_br.py`
- `tests/test_tracker_surface.py`
payload.title: Decode subprocess output as utf-8 explicitly so a capture never swallows the error

payload.name: description
payload.value:
## The defect, re-measured 2026-08-19

The original record named four files and **all four are gone**: the engine module for the retired binary, a tracker surface module, and their two tests. The code moved, so the record read as stale. The concern is not stale, and the shape has changed.

**The correct fix already exists.** `src/basicly/checkout.py` line 76 defines a shared wrapper that passes `encoding="utf-8"` explicitly, and its docstring names the reason: Windows defaults to cp1252. `checkout.git` routes every git call through it. That half is done and should not be re-done.

**What is live is the set of call sites that bypass the wrapper.** Measured over the engine, the kit and the gate scripts: **20 direct subprocess call sites construct their own call and pass no encoding**, so each decodes with the platform default.

Three of the twenty are in the agent dispatch path, `src/basicly/runner.py` at lines 692, 979 and 1501. That is the path that reads an agent stream, so on a platform whose default codec is not utf-8 an agent reply containing a non ascii byte decodes wrongly or raises, and the failure is attributed to the agent rather than to the decode. This repository declares Windows as a supported platform, so the exposure is real rather than theoretical.

The remaining seventeen are in the hook runner, the command line surface, the supervisor, the demonstration proof runner and nine gate scripts.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read the shared wrapper and confirm it passes an explicit encoding.
2. Search the engine, the kit and the gate scripts for a direct subprocess construction.
3. For each, check whether the call passes an encoding. Observe twenty that do not.
4. Positive control: the same probe finds the two sites that do pass one, so the probe discriminates.

Observed: twenty call sites decode subprocess output with the platform default while a correct shared wrapper exists beside them.
Expected: a call site either routes through the shared wrapper or states its own explicit encoding.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a subprocess call site in the engine or the kit or a gate script when it captures text then it routes through the shared wrapper or passes an explicit encoding.
- Given a call site that genuinely needs bytes rather than text when it is reviewed then it says so at the call and is not counted as a defect.
- Given the agent dispatch path when it reads an agent reply containing a non ascii byte then the reply decodes identically on every supported platform.
- Given a new call site added later that passes no encoding then a check refuses it rather than letting it land.
- Given the count when the work completes then the record states the expected and actual remaining count and they agree.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/hooks.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/demonstration_proof.py`
- `.scripts/ratchet.py`
- `.scripts/wired_or_deleted.py`
- `.scripts/check_test_naming.py`
- `.scripts/check_tree_growth.py`
- `.scripts/kit_deployment.py`
- `.scripts/generate_release_changelog.py`

## Trigger

When a subprocess call site decodes with the platform default instead of the shared utf-8 wrapper, I want it to route through checkout's wrapper or pass an explicit encoding, so I can stop a non-ascii agent reply from decoding wrongly or being blamed on the agent.

## The defect, re-measured 2026-08-19

The original record named four files and **all four are gone**: the engine module for the retired binary, a tracker surface module, and their two tests. The code moved, so the record read as stale. The concern is not stale, and the shape has changed.

**The correct fix already exists.** `src/basicly/checkout.py` line 76 defines a shared wrapper that passes `encoding="utf-8"` explicitly, and its docstring names the reason: Windows defaults to cp1252. `checkout.git` routes every git call through it. That half is done and should not be re-done.

**What is live is the set of call sites that bypass the wrapper.** Measured over the engine, the kit and the gate scripts: **20 direct subprocess call sites construct their own call and pass no encoding**, so each decodes with the platform default.

Three of the twenty are in the agent dispatch path, `src/basicly/runner.py` at lines 692, 979 and 1501. That is the path that reads an agent stream, so on a platform whose default codec is not utf-8 an agent reply containing a non ascii byte decodes wrongly or raises, and the failure is attributed to the agent rather than to the decode. This repository declares Windows as a supported platform, so the exposure is real rather than theoretical.

The remaining seventeen are in the hook runner, the command line surface, the supervisor, the demonstration proof runner and nine gate scripts.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read the shared wrapper and confirm it passes an explicit encoding.
2. Search the engine, the kit and the gate scripts for a direct subprocess construction.
3. For each, check whether the call passes an encoding. Observe twenty that do not.
4. Positive control: the same probe finds the two sites that do pass one, so the probe discriminates.

Observed: twenty call sites decode subprocess output with the platform default while a correct shared wrapper exists beside them.
Expected: a call site either routes through the shared wrapper or states its own explicit encoding.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/hooks.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/demonstration_proof.py`
- `.scripts/ratchet.py`
- `.scripts/wired_or_deleted.py`
- `.scripts/check_test_naming.py`
- `.scripts/check_tree_growth.py`
- `.scripts/kit_deployment.py`
- `.scripts/generate_release_changelog.py`
- `.scripts/recall_eval.py`
- `.scripts/setup_git_identity.py`
- `tests/test_runner.py`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given a subprocess call site in the engine or the kit or a gate script when it captures text then it routes through the shared wrapper or passes an explicit encoding.
- Given a call site that genuinely needs bytes rather than text when it is reviewed then it says so at the call and is not counted as a defect.
- Given the agent dispatch path when it reads an agent reply containing a non ascii byte then the reply decodes identically on every supported platform.
- Given a new call site added later that passes no encoding then a check refuses it rather than letting it land.
- Given the count when the work completes then the record states the expected and actual remaining count and they agree.

WHEN a new call site passes no encoding, a check SHALL refuse it, and a genuine bytes-only call SHALL say so at the call rather than count as a defect.

payload.description:
## Context

Observed 2026-08-22 during a four-lane supervised pass. `git status --short` in the base checkout reported:

```text
?? .basicly/ledger/.events.lock
```

## The file is transient and unignored

`.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py:176` declares `LOCK_NAME = ".events.lock"`. The file is created and removed around a ledger write, so it exists only for the width of one append. The reading above caught a lane mid-write against the shared ledger.

It is **not** matched by any rule in `.gitignore`, confirmed with `git check-ignore -v`.

## Why this is worth a line

`.gitignore` states the governing rule twice in its own comments, at line 47 - *an untracked one would block every landing (basicly-jr0l.7)* - and at line 81 - *a checkout carries dirt outside the tracker, so an untracked one blocks every landing*. Both were written about exactly this class of file. `.basicly/ledger/snapshot.jsonl`, `checkpoint-*.jsonl` and `redirect` are all ignored on that reasoning; the lock is the one member of the family that was missed.

The exposure is a race, not a standing failure: a base-cleanliness check that samples during an append sees a dirty tree and refuses. With one writer the window is negligible. With four lanes writing a shared ledger it is not, and the failure it produces is a landing refused for a file that has already ceased to exist - which is the hardest kind to diagnose, because reproducing it means catching the same window.

## Not yet fixed, and why

`.gitignore` is on this repository's explicit-confirmation list. The one-line rule is not applied here.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN the tracker holds its append lock, A CLEANLINESS CHECK OF THE BASE CHECKOUT SHALL NOT report the checkout dirty.
- WHEN the rule is added, IT SHALL name the lock exactly and SHALL NOT widen to a pattern that could hide a real ledger file.
- WHERE the rule is added, A COMMENT SHALL state why, consistent with the two neighbouring comments that state the same rule.

## Scope

- `.gitignore`

## Plan

- integrity: `L1`
- budget: `20000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: Hold the tracker's append lock, run the base cleanliness check, and read a clean verdict, against a control run with a genuinely untracked file present that must still report dirty.
